UP PLAYBOOK 2026
CD-S-002
Corporate Communications Strategy
Strategy Building scope. Sibling workflow to CD-S-001.
Version 1.0 | April 2026
Owner: Chief Strategy Officer
Approver: CEO
Note. This workflow follows the same template structure as CD-S-001 and references it for common elements. Where CD-S-002 says "as per CD-S-001," that material is identical. Where it differs, the differences are explicit and material — that's where corporate strategy work meaningfully diverges from brand work.
Section 1 — Identification
Section 2 — Purpose & Scope
Purpose. To produce a client-approved corporate communications strategy that defines how the company (not its individual brands) will build, protect, and grow its reputation with all material stakeholders — investors, regulators, employees, media, government, NGOs, customers, partners, and the public — through integrated communications across earned, owned, shared, and selectively paid channels.
A corporate strategy at UP is PR-centric, stakeholder-led, reputation-driven. It is the highest-stakes work UP does because corporate reputation directly affects company valuation, license to operate, employee engagement, and commercial outcomes. The 2026 UP deck explicitly cites that brand and corporate reputation can account for 15% to 30% of a company's total valuation — and up to 40% for companies with strong identity and trust. That number is the value at stake in this workflow.
In scope
Corporate reputation strategies for established companies (e.g. Diageo as the parent of Johnnie Walker; Melexis as a corporate; VMware as the regional employer and innovator)
Repositioning of the corporate identity (e.g. post-merger, post-leadership-change, post-crisis)
Annual corporate communications strategy refresh for retained clients
Corporate strategy work for B2B companies where the company is the brand (e.g. SAAB, Fadata, Linamar, Kyndryl)
Corporate strategy for Bulgarian companies expanding internationally (intersects with CD-S-004 Market Entry)
Corporate strategy for international companies entering or scaling in the markets UP serves
Out of scope
Brand-level strategy → use CD-S-001 Brand Communications Strategy
Strategies that must address brand and corporate together → use CD-S-003 Integrated Alignment
Pure public affairs / regulatory engagement strategies → use CD-S-010 Public Affairs Strategy (which can also nest as a component here)
Live crisis events → use CD-E-013 Crisis Live Response
Pitch-stage corporate work for prospects → compressed pitch workflow
Mode clarification
Corporate Communications Strategy is standalone-only. It defines the overall reputation objective and stakeholder universe; it cannot be a component of another strategy. The dual-mode strategies that nest inside a Corporate Strategy as components are listed in Section 5 Step 3.3.
When to use this workflow
A new corporate client signs UP for reputation work
An existing retainer client commissions an annual corporate strategy refresh
A material corporate event invalidates the existing strategy: M&A, leadership change, restructuring, IPO/delisting, regulatory action, ESG transition, geopolitical exposure
A standalone corporate engagement is commissioned (e.g. positioning around a major investment, reputation rebuild, ESG transition)
The client faces a multi-stakeholder challenge that brand-level work cannot solve
When NOT to use this workflow
Single-product or single-brand work — use CD-S-001
Tactical media engagement around a specific moment without underlying strategy — use CD-E-004 Media Relations Planning & Execution
Issues management without strategic context — use CD-E-013 Crisis Live Response if live, or CD-S-007 Crisis Preparedness if proactive
Section 3 — Inputs
Largely as per CD-S-001, with the following corporate-specific additions and elevations:
Quality gate principle, intensified. For corporate work, input quality directly correlates with strategic accuracy. A brand strategy with weak inputs produces mediocre work. A corporate strategy with weak inputs produces dangerously wrong work — recommendations that fail under regulatory scrutiny, stakeholder pushback, or analyst challenge. Strategy Lead has hard veto authority on input quality.
Section 4 — Roles & RACI
Largely as per CD-S-001, with these corporate-specific elevations:
Two key clarifications corporate strategy demands
Senior leadership is non-optional. A corporate strategy without senior co-leadership is a brand strategy mislabeled. UP's CEO and CSO are part of the product the client is buying.
Legal must be in the loop early on regulated work. Late legal review at the end of Phase 4 has killed otherwise good corporate strategies. For regulated clients, legal is consulted at insight definition, not just at presentation.
Section 5 — Process Steps
The five-phase structure of CD-S-001 holds, but the content of each phase shifts substantially. The biggest differences are in Phase 2 (research goes deeper into stakeholders and regulatory context), Phase 3 (the components and frameworks differ), and Phase 4 (legal and ethical review is heavier).
Phase 1 — Immersion & Discovery (Week 1)
As per CD-S-001 Phase 1, with these adjustments:
Step 1.1 Client kickoff must include the corporate decision-maker (CEO, CommsDir, or board sponsor), not only working-level contacts. If the decision-maker is unavailable for kickoff, kickoff is rescheduled, not held without them. This is a hard rule.
Step 1.3 Background immersion explicitly includes: annual reports, investor calls and transcripts, analyst reports, employee survey data, regulatory filings, prior crisis records, and any pending or recent legal matters. AI summarization is permitted within Section 9 boundaries — typically much narrower for corporate clients than for brand.
New step 1.5 — Legal & compliance context briefing. For regulated, listed, or high-stakes clients, the Strategy Lead briefs legal counsel (internal client legal or external) on the engagement and confirms what cannot be communicated externally during the strategy period. Establishes the disclosure perimeter early.
Phase 2 — Research & Insight (Weeks 1–4, longer than brand)
This is where corporate strategy diverges most sharply from brand strategy. Research is deeper, broader, more stakeholder-oriented, and more rigorous.
Step 2.1 — Business & operating context audit
(Replaces "category audit".) Financial performance, operating model, geographic footprint, M&A history, governance, ESG posture, regulatory exposure, key risks disclosed in annual report. Output: business and operating context summary.
Step 2.2 — Stakeholder universe mapping
(Elevated and expanded vs CD-S-001.) The most important phase of corporate research. Comprehensive identification and segmentation:
The deliverable uses the influence/interest grid for prioritization. Output: comprehensive stakeholder map.
Step 2.3 — Reputation audit
Detailed assessment of current corporate reputation across stakeholder groups. Sources include: media coverage analysis (volume, sentiment, narratives, share of voice vs competitors), social listening across professional platforms (LinkedIn, X, sector forums) and general platforms, analyst sentiment, employee engagement scores if available, customer satisfaction data if available, NGO and regulatory commentary. Sensika and Media Zoom configured for corporate-mode listening (different from brand-mode). Output: reputation audit deck.
Step 2.4 — Competitive corporate audit
Reputation, narrative, ESG positioning, executive visibility, thought leadership posture, and crisis history of 3–5 named corporate peers. Distinct from brand competitive audit. Output: competitive corporate audit.
Step 2.5 — Regulatory & policy environment scan
Critical and corporate-specific. What regulatory, legislative, and policy developments will shape the company's operating environment over the strategy period? Coordinated with FTI Consulting or CEC Group via UP's public affairs partnerships when relevant. Output: regulatory & policy memo.
Step 2.6 — Issues & vulnerability scan
What are the company's foreseeable reputation vulnerabilities? Past issues, ongoing litigation, sector controversies, ESG exposures, leadership exposures, geographic risk, supply chain risk, AI/data exposure (a 2026 universal). This is not crisis preparedness (CD-S-007) — this is strategic awareness of the vulnerability landscape that the strategy must address. Output: vulnerability register.
Step 2.7 — Cultural & geopolitical scan
For 2026, geopolitical context (energy transition, supply chain reshoring, EU regulatory leadership, US-China dynamics, defense reorientation in CEE) is integral to corporate strategy. Trends, cultural forces, and political shifts that will shape the company's operating reality. Output: cultural and geopolitical memo.
Step 2.8 — Insight synthesis
Strategy Lead synthesizes all research into 1–3 corporate insights that will drive the strategy. Corporate insights typically take the form of "what tension does this company need to resolve in the eyes of its stakeholders to grow / protect itself / earn license to operate?" The insight is always human-defined, never AI-generated. Output: corporate insight statement(s) logged in Insight Library.
Decision Point: Re-brief or proceed?
Same as CD-S-001 but with elevated stakes. If research reveals the original brief was wrong or incomplete on corporate matters — particularly if a material risk or regulatory issue surfaces that the client did not disclose at kickoff — the Strategy Lead pauses and re-engages the client. Proceeding with undisclosed material risk is not just a workflow failure; it's a professional ethics issue.
Phase 3 — Strategy Development (Weeks 4–6)
Step 3.1 — Strategic positioning
Define the company's strategic positioning across stakeholders. Different from a brand proposition — corporate positioning answers "what does this company stand for, deliver, and protect?" rather than "what does this brand mean to consumers?" Output: corporate positioning one-pager.
Step 3.2 — Corporate narrative & messaging architecture
Multi-track architecture, not single-message:
Master corporate narrative (one)
Audience-specific message tracks (per stakeholder segment — investor message track, employee message track, media message track, regulator message track, etc.)
Proof points per track
Tone of voice per track (regulator-facing language is not media-facing language)
"Do not say" guardrails — explicit messages to avoid for legal, regulatory, or reputational reasons
Output: messaging framework with multi-track architecture.
Step 3.3 — Stakeholder engagement approach — the Required Components
Where brand strategies are PESO-led, corporate strategies are stakeholder-led. Each stakeholder segment gets an explicit engagement approach. The required components for a corporate strategy are:
The components matrix is the quality checklist. A corporate strategy missing a required component is not complete.
Step 3.4 — Reputation measurement framework
Different from brand measurement. The framework typically combines:
Reputation tracking (RepTrak, brand-specific tracker, or commissioned tracking)
Share of voice and sentiment in tier-1 business media
Stakeholder-specific KPIs (analyst sentiment, employee engagement, regulator relationship indicators, NGO sentiment)
Issues resilience metrics
Executive visibility metrics
Thought leadership impact (citations, speaker invitations, content engagement)
Crisis-readiness indicators
Aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 (2025) and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework (IEF), but with a corporate framework rather than a brand framework. Mixed quantitative and qualitative methods are required (Barcelona Principle 3); AVEs are explicitly excluded (Barcelona Principle 4); outputs, outcomes and impact must all be reported (Barcelona Principle 5); and ethics, governance and transparency in data and methodology are documented (Barcelona Principle 6). Output: corporate measurement framework.
Step 3.5 — Phased budget allocation
Corporate budgets typically skew earned and owned, with selective paid for executive thought leadership and major moments. Production costs (research papers, content hubs, signature events) are often substantial and need explicit treatment. Output: budget table.
Step 3.6 — Risk register & mitigation
More extensive than for brand work. Strategic risks, reputational risks, regulatory risks, legal risks, ethical risks, geopolitical risks. Output: risk register.
Step 3.7 — Annual roadmap
Twelve-month corporate calendar showing major moments (results announcements, investor days, AGM, sustainability report publication, executive appearances, signature events, anticipated regulatory milestones), plus always-on activity. Output: roadmap.
Step 3.8 — Internal alignment plan
Corporate-specific: how will this strategy be socialized inside the client organization? Who needs to buy in beyond the immediate sponsor? Corporate strategies fail more often from internal misalignment than from external rejection. Output: internal alignment plan.
Phase 4 — Internal Review & Packaging (Week 6–7)
As per CD-S-001 Phase 4, with these elevations:
Internal challenge session is mandatory and senior-led. CEO and CSO co-lead the challenge for all corporate strategies. For flagship corporate engagements, an external senior advisor may be invited.
New step — Legal review. For regulated, listed, or high-stakes corporate strategies, the strategy is reviewed by legal counsel before client presentation. Specifically: disclosure perimeter compliance, MNPI considerations, regulatory positioning, litigation posture coherence.
New step — Ethical review. For corporate strategies touching geopolitical, defense, healthcare, public-sector, or politically sensitive matters, an explicit ethical review by a senior reviewer not involved in drafting. This is a real and increasingly important governance step in 2026.
Phase 5 — Client Presentation & Approval (Week 7–8)
As per CD-S-001 Phase 5, with these elevations:
Client presentation is to the decision-maker (CEO or board sponsor), not only the Communications Director.
CEO of UP attends in person for new corporate clients, flagship engagements, or strategies above the value threshold.
Approval is in writing, formally archived. Corporate strategy approval is signed-document-grade, not email-grade.
Internal client launch. Corporate strategies require an internal launch within the client organization. UP supports this — typically through an internal launch deck, town hall support, and an internal Q&A pack.
Handover triggers. As per CD-S-001, plus typically multiple component-mode strategies (CD-S-007 Crisis, CD-S-008 Employer, CD-S-011 Executive Profiling, CD-S-012 CSR) trigger downstream depending on the components.
Section 6 — Outputs & Deliverables
Section 7 — Systems & Tools
As per CD-S-001, with these corporate-specific notes:
Sensika and Media Zoom configured for corporate listening — different keyword sets, different sources, different dashboards from brand-mode. Set up at engagement start; don't reuse a brand listening config for corporate work.
Bloomberg, Reuters, FT, S&P / Moody's databases — for listed clients, access to financial intelligence sources is required for credible work.
LinkedIn Sales Navigator and equivalent — for stakeholder mapping at named-individual level.
Approved AI tools for corporate work — narrower list than brand work. Some clients restrict AI tool use to EU-hosted only, named-providers only. The #AI-status field in the project file is set per client and enforced strictly.
Section 8 — AI Augmentation
The pattern from CD-S-001 holds, but the AI permissiveness is materially lower for corporate work.
AI today — what UP does in corporate work
Document summarization — annual reports, regulatory filings, analyst reports synthesized into immersion memos. Strategist validates anything entering the strategy.
Stakeholder universe research acceleration — initial stakeholder identification from public sources.
Reputation audit synthesis — themes extracted from media and social listening data.
Regulatory environment scanning — initial scan accelerated; legal-relevant interpretation always human and where warranted, lawyer-validated.
Drafting support — narrative drafts, deck copy. Always human-authored in final form.
Insight stress-testing — AI as a thinking partner challenging assumptions.
AI next — corporate-specific roadmap
Continuous reputation monitoring with stakeholder-specific signal detection (E: H, I: H). Move from monthly audit to continuous monitoring with early warning for stakeholder-specific risks.
Analyst sentiment tracking automation for listed clients (E: M, I: H).
Regulatory development tracking with semantic alerting (E: H, I: H). Critical for regulated clients in 2026.
Stakeholder-specific message tracking — does the messaging architecture actually land with each segment? AI-assisted analysis of received vs intended messages.
Synthetic stakeholder simulation — testing messages with simulated stakeholder personas before exposure. Higher value but also higher risk; deploy carefully.
Human-in-the-loop requirements — even firmer than for brand
The corporate insight is always human and always defended by senior judgment. Corporate insights affect company valuation and license to operate. AI proposes; humans decide and own.
Anything stakeholder-facing is human-reviewed. Every word, every visual, every framing. No exceptions.
Material non-public information (MNPI) is never processed in AI tools. For listed clients, this is a legal requirement, not a preference.
Regulatory and legal recommendations require legal review — not just human review. For regulated work, a non-lawyer human reviewing legal-relevant content is not sufficient governance.
Ethical review is mandatory for corporate strategies touching geopolitical, defense, public-sector, healthcare, or politically sensitive matters.
#noAI variant is the default for: listed clients during quiet periods, M&A engagements, regulated-sector clients with restrictive contracts, public-sector clients, defense clients, and any client who has explicitly opted out.
Audit trail is mandatory and elevated. Prompt logs retained for the contract duration plus 7 years (longer than brand workflow's 3 years), reflecting the longer regulatory and legal tail of corporate work. Aligned with Barcelona Principle 7 — ethics, governance and transparency with data, methodologies and technology builds trust and drives learning.
Failure modes specific to corporate AI use — and they're severe
MNPI leak via AI prompt — career-ending and potentially regulatory.
Hallucinated regulatory citation in a strategy document — exposes UP and the client to sanction.
AI-generated "executive voice" content that doesn't match the executive — visible, embarrassing, and undermines trust at exactly the wrong level.
Stakeholder data processed without proper consent — GDPR and ePrivacy exposure.
Cross-client MNPI exposure — Client A's listed-company information surfaces in Client B's work. Catastrophic.
These risks are why corporate AI use at UP is conservative by design.
Section 9 — Data & Compliance
Data classifications handled
Most corporate strategy work defaults to Restricted.
M&A, pre-results-period, IPO/delisting, restructuring, and major regulatory engagements default to Highly Restricted.
Public-sector, defense, and healthcare work frequently elevates to Highly Restricted.
MNPI handling for listed clients
Quiet periods enforced — strategy work paused or limited around results announcements per the client's disclosure calendar.
AI tool use restricted or prohibited during quiet periods.
Need-to-know access enforced — corporate strategy team for listed clients is a named, limited group.
All team members on listed-client work confirm in writing they understand MNPI obligations. Logged annually.
GDPR considerations for corporate work
Stakeholder mapping at named-individual level requires GDPR-compliant handling.
Employee research and engagement data is high-sensitivity.
Cross-border data flows in multi-market corporate work require explicit safeguards.
EU AI Act alignment, 2026
Most corporate communications work is limited-risk under the AI Act.

# Real Client Case For AI Workflow Demo

Selected case: Corporate brand strategy, built from scratch

Client: A real United Partners telecom client, sanitized. No client name is used.

Status: Sanitized, confidential, for AI workflow demo.

## Short Ask

This case is a corporate brand and corporate communications strategy built from a blank slate. The client has no approved corporate brand strategy, and positioning, narrative, and pillar architecture are not pre-decided. The workflow must reason from evidence to a defensible strategy and show what is fact, what is missing, and what is strategic judgment.

## Client Type

Industry/category: Telecommunications: fixed line, mobile, broadband internet, TV/entertainment, and B2B solutions such as IoT, smart cities, cloud, and digital education.

Market/country: A single mid-sized European national market. The client is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group.

B2B or B2C: Both. Mass-market consumer is the revenue core. B2B, enterprise, and public-sector solutions are strategic growth areas.

Current business situation: Market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator. Operationally strong, with leading network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets. Stable and profitable, but operating in a mature, saturated, price-pressured market where the three main operators have converged on near-identical positioning. The company operates beyond core connectivity, but is not yet recognized for that broader role.

## Real Challenge

Trigger: A leadership transition requiring a narrative reset. The specific transition details are excluded from AI use.

What the client wants to change: Move from reactive, campaign-by-campaign communications to one coherent corporate brand strategy. The client must decide on a corporate positioning and narrative that do not currently exist in approved form. Prior agency proposals were liked but never adopted, so the company is effectively starting fresh.

Business/reputation problem:

- Differentiation: the three main operators recycle technology leadership, ESG, and employer-brand claims.
- Affinity: the category is trusted but not loved.
- Contested leadership: share of voice has moved from clear dominance to a tight race.
- Latent strength: national scale, infrastructure, digital-economy role, CSR, and skills programmes exist, but are communicated as episodes rather than one corporate story.

## Objectives

- Re-establish corporate reputation and leadership trust after the transition.
- Build a differentiated corporate brand platform the market can recognize.
- Lift affinity and preference in a trusted-but-not-loved category.
- Strengthen employer brand for digital and engineering talent.
- Establish credible, ownable ESG and societal-contribution leadership.

## Audiences To Prioritize

These audiences are not pre-ranked. The strategy must prioritize them.

- Media: national news, business/financial press, tech media, consumer media.
- Regulators, policy stakeholders, and government stakeholders.
- Talent and future talent: students, STEM graduates, tech community.
- Business and enterprise customers and partners.
- General public and consumer base.
- Parent-group corporate stakeholders.

## Must-Say And Must-Avoid

Because positioning is open, these are guardrails, not the message itself.

Must-say guardrails:

- Use verifiable and ownable proof.
- Show a genuine role in the country’s digital progress.
- Build one company story rather than disconnected activity claims.

Must-avoid guardrails:

- Do not fall back into state-utility or former-monopoly framing.
- Do not recycle shared category claims around technology leadership, ESG, or employer branding as the central idea.
- Do not use competitive price-war messaging as corporate positioning.
- Do not introduce political framing.

## Decision Setup

Primary approval owner: client-side Corporate Communications lead.

Final sign-off: CEO and parent-group corporate communications function.

Consulted teams: Marketing, HR/People, Product, Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and parent-group communications.

Internal alignment tension: Marketing owns consumer brand and advertising budget. Corporate Communications owns reputation and PR. The corporate platform must sit above and feed consumer campaigns without colliding with them. Parent-group requirements add an approval layer. Because positioning is genuinely undecided, the strategy must force and document the positioning decision the client still owes itself.

## Competitive And Market Context

Main competitors: two strong rivals in a three-player market. One is positioned around technology/network leadership and social-impact programming. The other is positioned around customer experience and independently certified network quality. Both invest heavily in corporate narrative and are closing the share-of-voice gap.

Reference brands: major European incumbent operators that repositioned from utility to digital enabler. These are directional benchmarks only, not targets to copy.

Market pressure: mature, saturated, price-competitive market; streaming pressure on traditional TV consumption; convergence pressure from over-the-top players. Growth must come from preference and value, not volume.

Known audience-perception problem: the category is trusted but not admired. The client is respected for reliability and scale but is not associated with a distinctive idea. Competitors out-narrate it on innovation and customer experience, while the client’s relative strength appears more in corporate, sustainability, and CSR coverage than product buzz.

Open strategic question: Is incumbent scale and infrastructure a liability to move away from, or, retold in human and national terms, the one position rivals cannot match? The strategy must take a view; the brief must not assume one.

## Channels And Components

PESO direction:

- Earned: core driver for corporate reputation.
- Owned: newsroom, reports, internal channels, and thought-leadership content.
- Shared: professional social, executive social, consumer social where relevant.
- Paid: supporting role only.
- Partnerships, CSR, and ESG: high relevance.
- Crisis sensitivity: regulatory proceedings, outages, data security, and leadership-transition sensitivities.

## Constraints

Legal/regulatory:

- The client operates under a national communications regulator.
- Claims touching market share, pricing, or competitive position require Legal/Regulatory review.
- ESG claims must align with group-verified data.
- GDPR applies to audience targeting, campaign data, and influencer data handling.
- EU AI Act, DSA, and DMA awareness is required where relevant.

AI-use limits:

- Exclude leadership-transition specifics.
- Exclude real commercial or retainer terms.
- Exclude competitor-by-name intelligence.
- Exclude unannounced strategic plans.
- Use only publicly grounded facts plus this sanitized brief.
- Treat prior unadopted agency positioning ideas as tone reference only, never approved positioning.
- Replace client and individual names with generic stand-ins or role titles.
- Replace financial specifics, budgets, and retainer terms with ranges or TBC.

## Expected Outputs

- Evidence base and readiness check: what is known, what is missing, and what must be decided before strategy can proceed.
- Positioning options: two to three reasoned territories with a recommended direction and rationale, not a single pre-baked answer.
- Corporate brand platform/message architecture: core idea, narrative, and message house framed as a first build for client decision.
- Pillar architecture: derived from evidence and argued, including how many pillars and why.
- Stakeholder and executive thought-leadership map.
- Twelve-month roadmap/campaign platform linked to business moments.
- Measurement framework aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework.

## What Good Looks Like

- Input discipline: surfaces gaps before writing and flags that positioning is undecided.
- Strategic structure: pillars and positioning are reasoned from evidence, not borrowed from competitors.
- Review trail: every recommendation traces to input and separates fact from judgment.
- Honest about unsettled decisions: presents options for client decision rather than asserting a finished answer.
- Practical first artifact: message architecture small enough for a client decision meeting, but substantive enough to test the central strategic bet.

## Safety Note

This brief uses sanitized facts plus publicly grounded context. No confidential client documents, real names, real financials, or specifics of the leadership transition are included. The strategic problem is preserved while identifying and sensitive details are removed or generalized. The account team should review anything pulled into a live demo before it runs.

# Pre-Engagement Briefing Pack

What we know about this client before anyone speaks to them. Six audits from the material available, a provisional point of view to be argued with, and a read of how the client writes about itself.

Anything an audit could not confirm is listed as a gap rather than stated as a finding.

**Format.** 6 short audit sections and a one-paragraph hypothesis, 3–5 pages.

## Business audit

- The client is a telecommunications company offering fixed line, mobile, broadband internet, TV/entertainment, and B2B solutions including IoT, smart cities, cloud, and digital education (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The client operates in a single mid-sized European national market and is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The client is described as the market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator, with strong network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The client's market is described as mature, saturated, price-pressured, and converged around similar claims among three main operators (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- Connect Europe reports that the European telecoms market is increasingly mature and that competitive pressure limits operators' ability to offset inflation through price rises (https://connecteurope.org/insights/reports/state-digital-communications-2025)

Still to check:
- No public client identity was supplied, so revenue, subscriber base, market share, ownership structure, capex, margin, and exact operating footprint could not be verified.
- The leadership transition trigger is intentionally excluded from AI use, so its timing, public salience, and reputational effect could not be assessed.
- No annual report, investor deck, regulator filings, or parent-group disclosures for the named company were available in the supplied material.

## Reputation audit

- The client has no approved corporate brand strategy and must build positioning, narrative, and pillar architecture from evidence (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The supplied brief says the client is respected for reliability and scale but is not associated with a distinctive idea (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The supplied brief says the category is trusted but not admired and that the client needs to lift affinity and preference (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The supplied brief says share of voice has moved from clear dominance to a tight race (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- Caliber identifies data security breaches, service disruptions, pricing sentiment, misleading marketing, and inadequate customer service as major telecom reputation risks (https://www.groupcaliber.com/sectors/telecoms-industry/)

Still to check:
- No media corpus, sentiment analysis, share-of-voice data, or narrative timeline was supplied.
- No stakeholder perception data was supplied for customers, employees, regulators, media, investors, or parent-group audiences.
- No issue history, outage record, regulatory proceeding history, or crisis archive was supplied.

## Social & digital audit

- The supplied brief identifies earned media as the core reputation driver, with owned, shared, paid, partnerships, CSR, and ESG playing supporting roles (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The UP corporate workflow defines the required corporate digital and social approach as LinkedIn-first and differentiated from brand social (CD-S-002_Corporate_Communications_Strategy.docx)
- The supplied brief identifies executive thought leadership as an expected output through a stakeholder and executive thought-leadership map (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- Edelman and LinkedIn's 2025 B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report says thought leadership is used to build trust, drive alignment, and open doors in complex buying groups (https://www.edelman.com/expertise/Business-Marketing/2025-b2b-thought-leadership-report)
- The European Commission describes the Digital Services Act as regulating online services and platforms to create a safer digital space with protected fundamental rights (https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/digital-services-act-keeping-us-safe-online-2025-09-22_en)

Still to check:
- The client's actual LinkedIn, executive social, newsroom, corporate website, and social engagement performance could not be audited because the identity is sanitized.
- No channel analytics, follower data, engagement rates, content themes, paid-media data, or listening dashboards were supplied.
- No evidence was supplied on whether executives are visible, credible, or silent in public digital channels.

## Competitive audit

- The supplied brief says the market has two strong rivals in a three-player structure (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- One rival is described as positioned around technology/network leadership and social-impact programming (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The other rival is described as positioned around customer experience and independently certified network quality (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- Deutsche Telekom states a strategic ambition to be the leading digital telecommunications company and frames itself as a reliable partner for customers, society, and the environment (https://www.telekom.com/en/company/strategy/details/group-strategy-515316)
- Orange's 2026-2030 strategy is built around customer proximity, innovative growth, and excellence at scale under the platform 'Trust the Future' (https://www.orange.com/en/our-group/our-strategy)

Still to check:
- Competitor names, live campaigns, current share of voice, investment levels, and claim substantiation could not be verified because competitor-by-name intelligence is excluded.
- No side-by-side corporate narrative, ESG, employer brand, executive visibility, or crisis-history comparison was supplied.
- No benchmark evidence was supplied showing which European incumbent repositioning models are relevant to this national market.

## Stakeholder scan

- Priority audiences named in the supplied brief are media, regulators, policy and government stakeholders, talent, business customers and partners, the general public and consumer base, and parent-group corporate stakeholders (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- Final sign-off sits with the CEO and parent-group corporate communications function, while the client-side Corporate Communications lead is the primary approval owner (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- Consulted teams include Marketing, HR/People, Product, Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and parent-group communications (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The supplied brief identifies an internal alignment tension between Marketing's ownership of consumer brand and advertising budget and Corporate Communications' ownership of reputation and PR (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The UP corporate workflow treats stakeholder universe mapping as the most important phase of corporate research and requires an influence/interest grid for prioritization (CD-S-002_Corporate_Communications_Strategy.docx)

Still to check:
- No named stakeholder map, influence/interest grid, decision-maker interview notes, or parent-group approval criteria were supplied.
- No regulator, policymaker, journalist, analyst, NGO, university, STEM-community, or enterprise-customer names were supplied.
- No evidence was supplied on which audience currently drives reputation risk or opportunity most strongly.

## Context scan

- The client operates under a national communications regulator, and claims about market share, pricing, or competitive position require Legal/Regulatory review (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The supplied brief requires ESG claims to align with group-verified data and requires GDPR awareness for audience targeting, campaign data, and influencer data handling (sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
- The European Commission's 2025 State of the Digital Decade report covers EU progress and challenges across digital transformation, including connectivity, AI, digital skills, and foundational technologies (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/state-digital-decade-2025-report)
- The European Commission says companies subject to CSRD must report according to European Sustainability Reporting Standards (https://finance.ec.europa.eu/financial-markets/company-reporting-and-auditing/company-reporting/corporate-sustainability-reporting_en)
- The European Commission published guidelines on Article 50 AI Act transparency obligations, which start applying on 2 August 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/guidelines-transparency-obligations-providers-and-deployers-ai-systems)

Still to check:
- The exact national regulatory agenda, active proceedings, spectrum issues, consumer-protection disputes, and cybersecurity obligations could not be established without the country and company name.
- The client's CSRD scope, materiality assessment, sustainability data, and parent-group assurance status were not supplied.
- No local geopolitical, labor-market, education, digital-skills, or media-market evidence was supplied for the specific country.

## Provisional hypothesis

Provisional means the research that follows can overturn it. It is written to be tested, not defended.

The reputation problem is not that the incumbent telecom lacks proof; it is that its strongest proof is trapped in infrastructure, CSR, skills, and national digital-economy activity that reads as disconnected corporate episodes, while competitors have turned narrower claims into clearer public stories. The white space is to reclaim incumbent scale as a human and national advantage: the company that makes digital progress usable, trusted, and locally consequential, without sliding back into former-utility nostalgia, generic network leadership, or political nation-building language.

**Confirmed if.** The hypothesis holds if media analysis, stakeholder interviews, and social listening find that audiences recognize the client's reliability, scale, CSR, and infrastructure role but cannot name a distinctive corporate idea, while competitors are more strongly associated with innovation or customer experience narratives.

**Overturned if.** The hypothesis is wrong if research finds that audiences already associate the client with a clear differentiated role beyond connectivity and that the main reputation barrier is instead product experience, price fairness, service frustration, or a specific unresolved trust event.

## Client Style Note (draft)

**Tone.** Analytical, controlled, governance-heavy, and explicit about risks, boundaries, and decision ownership.

**Sentence length.** Mostly medium to long, with short declarative lines used for rules, cautions, and quality gates.

**Vocabulary.** Corporate strategy, reputation, stakeholder, regulator, legal, governance, proof, narrative, positioning, ESG, AI, MNPI, measurement, risk, alignment.

**How they refer to themselves.** The material uses institutional third-person language and refers to roles, workflows, and the client rather than using a personal or promotional first-person voice.

**Signature words they use.** defensible, stakeholder-led, reputation-driven, license to operate, proof points, quality gate, risk register, human-defined insight, legal review, internal alignment

**Words that would read as wrong in their voice.** disruptive, game-changing, fun, cool, viral, cheap, political framing, former monopoly, price war, AI-generated insight

## Open — waiting on a person

These are not the engine's to make. The strategy does not proceed on a guess about either of them.

- **Which hypothesis do we test?** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.
- **Do we mirror the client's voice, or hold to house style? The volume's rule: mirror where strong, default to house style where not.** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.

**Length.** 3 pages at 500 words a page — within the 3–5 the volume asks for.

question_sets.title: essentials / the ask
questions: What is the one line about Vivacom you would personally defend in the room if we cannot use generic claims like technology leadership, ESG leadership, or employer brand?
What must this work produce first: a corporate positioning, an executive narrative, a proof architecture, a channel programme, or an internal alignment tool?

Which parts of Vivacom's current proof base are already safe to build on: first 5G, first 10-gigabit network, widest high-speed footprint by cities, unlimited plans, EON, CRC indicators, Opensignal, awards, or employer scale?
What does success need to change in people's heads: reliability recognition, emotional preference, innovation credibility, national relevance, or customer pride?
What should Vivacom stop being associated with immediately: the old BTK identity, former state-telecom inertia, overclaimed market leadership, or something else?
answered: The personally defensible line is: "You can't do without it."
Vivacom matters because its services let people do what matters most to them, in the best possible way, with connectivity anywhere, any time, and with everyone who matters.
The desired move is from moderate presence to more attractive, emotional, digital storytelling built around proof and quality content.
The company wants to cut association with "the BTK" and the old state-telecom identity.
Share of voice alone is not enough as a success measure.
follow_up: The formal deliverable hierarchy is still thin: positioning, proof ladder, executive platform, channel programme, and internal alignment are all implied but not prioritized.
The final business owner for the ask beyond the CCO is not established in the conversation material.
The hypothesis to test is still not formally chosen.

question_sets.title: business & organizational context
questions: Which Vivacom business lines most need the corporate narrative to lift: mobile, fixed, broadband, EON, Smart Home, B2B Smart City, cloud, education, or infrastructure?
Where has Vivacom genuinely moved the Bulgarian telecom market forward in ways competitors had to follow?
How should we describe the transformation from heavy incumbent to faster innovator without triggering old-state-operator associations?
How is the possible sale process affecting what leaders are willing to say internally and externally?
Which commercial proof points can be verified and paired with legal wording from the start?
answered: Vivacom is described as the most solid and stable telecom in Bulgaria that has stepped into the role of innovator.

Proof points supplied include first commercial 5G network in Bulgaria, first 10-gigabit network in Bulgaria, widest high-speed footprint by cities, first unlimited consumer plans, EON, CRC indicators, Opensignal, Forbes Innovation Awards, employer recognitions, and largest telecom employer status.
The transformation itself is seen as a genuine difference: a heavy incumbent that became faster and introduced innovations that moved the sector forward.
The sale context is creating strategic silence: leaders are waiting for a sale and piecemeal divestment due diligence, and "nobody dares say anything."
follow_up: Revenue, subscriber base, market share, margin, capex, and ownership details remain outside the supplied material.
The precise sale process, timing, public salience, and communication permissions are not established.
The business priority across consumer, enterprise, infrastructure, and entertainment is not ranked.

question_sets.title: reputation & stakeholder context
questions: Which reputation risk is most live for Vivacom now: BTK legacy, ownership-transition overhang, duct-network pressure, price indexation memory, Recovery and Resilience Plan scrutiny, regulator optics, or service disruptions from migrations?
Which stakeholder most constrains the story: regulators, government, Legal, parent-group communications, existing customers, critical urban audiences, competitors, or employees?
How should Vivacom handle market-leader proof without inviting regulator or government attention?
What can be said about national-critical infrastructure, satellite communications, and state services, and what must remain quarantined?
Which past shadows resurface when a sale process is visible, and what is the approved handling line?
answered: The BTK association must be cut categorically.
Boasting about being market leader across segments is discouraged because it invites regulator and government attention.
The duct network is an extra-care topic and a competitor attack vector.
The price-indexation scandal from about 2-3 years ago remains a competitor attack vector.
Ownership history involving the KTB, Tsvetan Vassilev, Delyan Peevski, and Spas Rusev chapters is a standing reputational overhang during visible sale processes.
Vendor-migration references are sensitive and must not be surfaced externally.
follow_up: No complete stakeholder risk ranking is supplied.
No approved handling language is supplied for duct network, ownership transition, state-layer national security, or vendor migration beyond Legal approval placeholders.
No media, regulator, customer, employee, or parent-group perception evidence is supplied.

question_sets.title: audience & insight
questions: Who must believe the new Vivacom story first: existing customers, critical urban audiences, Gen Z, employees, media, regulators, business customers, or parent-group stakeholders?
What would make existing customers re-see Vivacom after brand integrations, network migrations, and service disruption memories?
What is the emotional association Vivacom wants to create: indispensable, warm, innovative, local, useful, or personally part of people's journey?
What does the critical urban audience currently amplify for or against Vivacom?
What makes Gen Z only partly reached, and what proof or formats could close that gap?
answered: The first-believer audience is existing customers.
Existing customers lived through a bumpy road including brand integrations and network migrations, with noticeable disruptions.
Hardest audiences are existing customers and the critical urban audience, described as "the biggest influencer" for good and bad.
Gen Z is partially being reached but needs more.
The desired three-year association is people saying "Vivacom -- that's my telecom" or something short and warm like "my Vivacom, part of my journey."
follow_up: No audience research, segmentation, social listening, or sentiment evidence is supplied.
The current beliefs of existing customers, urban critics, Gen Z, business customers, media, regulators, and employees are not established beyond the CCO's read.
No quantified audience priority or influence/interest grid is supplied.

question_sets.title: programme, narrative & channels
questions: Which Vivacom stories should become the first narrative pillars: EON, Smart Home, B2B Smart City, Regional Grant, Job Lab, unlimited plans, 10-gigabit network, 5G, or customer-centred advertising?
How do we turn technical and CSR proof into a single human story rather than disconnected corporate episodes?
Which channels should carry the step-up: earned media, LinkedIn, executive visibility, owned newsroom, social video, internal town halls, partnerships, or product PR?
What does "more colourful, more digital, more attractive" mean in actual formats and cadence for a small comms team?
How should Vivacom measure reputation quality across traditional presence, social feedback, and sentiment?
answered: Under-told stories include the repositioned advertising approach putting the person at the centre of technology.
EON, Smart Home, and B2B Smart City solutions are under-told product and B2B stories.
Vivacom Regional Grant and Job Lab are personally important CSR and education stories.
The channel ambition is to tell success stories attractively, in more places and formats, so different people recognise themselves.
The desired content stance is middle boldness: step up from moderate presence, prioritize content quality over volume, and avoid flooding channels with low-quality material.
The desired measurement direction is a holistic instrument combining traditional presence with social-network feedback and sentiment.
follow_up: No final channel architecture is supplied.
No content calendar, resourcing model, format mix, or measurement methodology is established.
No decision is supplied on whether to mirror the client's voice or default to house style.

question_sets.title: team, culture & ways of working
questions: What internal behaviour must change for Vivacom's leaders to become credible public voices?
Which leaders are ready to step into company events, industry events, and social-responsibility topics, and which are still hesitant?
How should internal communications become livelier despite heavy internal systems?
What must be protected from the current culture: the experienced leadership team managing with heart, the cause-not-career commitment, and CEO-level customer engagement?
What can the small Corporate Communications team realistically own with UP's help?
answered: The experienced leadership team managing "with heart" feels true enough to keep.
For many leaders, Vivacom "is a cause, not a career."
Leadership should open up to the world and take active public roles in company events, industry events, and social-responsibility topics.
The barrier is leaders stepping out, even though "they have things to say."
The team is described as small but incredible, currently covering traditional PR channels at maximum capacity with UP's help.
Internal communications need a clear direction communicated to nearly all employees, better-designed regular content, more energy, and formats that bring leadership closer to people.
follow_up: No named leadership roster, readiness map, or executive thought-leadership ownership is supplied.
No operating model is supplied for how UP and the Corporate Communications team divide work.
No internal communications cadence, approvals flow, or tooling constraints are detailed beyond heavy systems.

question_sets.title: constraints & guardrails (incl. AI-use / MNPI)
questions: Which Vivacom claims require a legal-proof pair before use, especially around "first," "only," "widest," "best," market share, customer experience, and network quality?
Which proof points are public-record safe, which are Legal-approved, and which are quarantined until confirmed?
What must be excluded from AI-assisted drafting because it could involve MNPI, sale-process sensitivity, national-security sensitivity, vendor migration, or ownership-transition risk?
What is the approved rule for using flagged state-layer, satellite/teleport, duct-network, Recovery and Resilience Plan, and ownership-history material?
How should the team handle the competitor letter example around the single 10-gig site and the shift from "only" to "first"?
answered: Claims were re-audited and adapted from the start of the year with legal validation.
Vivacom can no longer say "the only" for the 10-gig claim; it can say "the first."
Every superlative needs a legal-proof pair.
Vendor-migration references must not be surfaced externally.
State-layer and national-security handling is flagged and quarantined until confirmed.
Duct network, Recovery and Resilience Plan projects, ownership history, market-leader boasting, and ownership-transition communication all require extra care.
follow_up: No full legal claim register is supplied.
No AI-use or MNPI protocol is supplied beyond the briefing pack's instruction that the leadership transition trigger is excluded from AI use.
No approved external wording is supplied for the flagged topics.
The "500 million" satellite/teleport reach figure is unclear and requires respondent confirmation.

What decision must happen first so the strategy can proceed: choose the hypothesis to test, approve the voice rule, confirm proof points, or define the stakeholder interview list?
What is the approval path for sensitive claims and flagged topics?
What is the timetable around the next town hall, possible sale-process milestones, and leadership visibility moments?
What capacity can the small Corporate Communications team commit to content management and channel expansion with UP's help?
answered: The CCO is the only respondent present in the supplied conversation material.
The CCO is trying to make leaders share visionary thinking at the next town hall.
Legal validation is required for contested claims and superlatives.
UP is already helping a small Corporate Communications team that is at maximum capacity on traditional PR channels.
follow_up: Final sign-off roles from the briefing pack are not confirmed in the conversation material.

No owner is recorded for choosing the hypothesis to test or deciding whether to mirror client voice or use house style.

# Debrief Write-Up

What the conversation established, tracked against the eight question sets, and what is still missing from each. A set with nothing under it was not covered -- that is a finding, not an omission from this document.

**Voices heard.** Elitza Georgieva (Chief Communications Officer)  Only one voice. The volume asks for more than one where possible.

## A — essentials / the ask

What we now know:
- The personally defensible line is: "You can't do without it."
- Vivacom matters because its services let people do what matters most to them, in the best possible way, with connectivity anywhere, any time, and with everyone who matters.
- The desired move is from moderate presence to more attractive, emotional, digital storytelling built around proof and quality content.
- The company wants to cut association with "the BTK" and the old state-telecom identity.
- Share of voice alone is not enough as a success measure.

Still to get:
- The formal deliverable hierarchy is still thin: positioning, proof ladder, executive platform, channel programme, and internal alignment are all implied but not prioritized.
- The final business owner for the ask beyond the CCO is not established in the conversation material.
- The hypothesis to test is still not formally chosen.

Questions for this set:

- What is the one line about Vivacom you would personally defend in the room if we cannot use generic claims like technology leadership, ESG leadership, or employer brand?
- What must this work produce first: a corporate positioning, an executive narrative, a proof architecture, a channel programme, or an internal alignment tool?
- Which parts of Vivacom's current proof base are already safe to build on: first 5G, first 10-gigabit network, widest high-speed footprint by cities, unlimited plans, EON, CRC indicators, Opensignal, awards, or employer scale?
- What does success need to change in people's heads: reliability recognition, emotional preference, innovation credibility, national relevance, or customer pride?
- What should Vivacom stop being associated with immediately: the old BTK identity, former state-telecom inertia, overclaimed market leadership, or something else?

## B — business & organizational context

What we now know:
- Vivacom is described as the most solid and stable telecom in Bulgaria that has stepped into the role of innovator.
- Proof points supplied include first commercial 5G network in Bulgaria, first 10-gigabit network in Bulgaria, widest high-speed footprint by cities, first unlimited consumer plans, EON, CRC indicators, Opensignal, Forbes Innovation Awards, employer recognitions, and largest telecom employer status.
- The transformation itself is seen as a genuine difference: a heavy incumbent that became faster and introduced innovations that moved the sector forward.
- The sale context is creating strategic silence: leaders are waiting for a sale and piecemeal divestment due diligence, and "nobody dares say anything."

Still to get:
- Revenue, subscriber base, market share, margin, capex, and ownership details remain outside the supplied material.
- The precise sale process, timing, public salience, and communication permissions are not established.
- The business priority across consumer, enterprise, infrastructure, and entertainment is not ranked.

Questions for this set:

- Which Vivacom business lines most need the corporate narrative to lift: mobile, fixed, broadband, EON, Smart Home, B2B Smart City, cloud, education, or infrastructure?
- Where has Vivacom genuinely moved the Bulgarian telecom market forward in ways competitors had to follow?
- How should we describe the transformation from heavy incumbent to faster innovator without triggering old-state-operator associations?
- How is the possible sale process affecting what leaders are willing to say internally and externally?
- Which commercial proof points can be verified and paired with legal wording from the start?

## C — reputation & stakeholder context

What we now know:
- The BTK association must be cut categorically.
- Boasting about being market leader across segments is discouraged because it invites regulator and government attention.
- The duct network is an extra-care topic and a competitor attack vector.
- The price-indexation scandal from about 2-3 years ago remains a competitor attack vector.
- Ownership history involving the KTB, Tsvetan Vassilev, Delyan Peevski, and Spas Rusev chapters is a standing reputational overhang during visible sale processes.
- Vendor-migration references are sensitive and must not be surfaced externally.

Still to get:
- No complete stakeholder risk ranking is supplied.
- No approved handling language is supplied for duct network, ownership transition, state-layer national security, or vendor migration beyond Legal approval placeholders.
- No media, regulator, customer, employee, or parent-group perception evidence is supplied.

Questions for this set:

- Which reputation risk is most live for Vivacom now: BTK legacy, ownership-transition overhang, duct-network pressure, price indexation memory, Recovery and Resilience Plan scrutiny, regulator optics, or service disruptions from migrations?
- Which stakeholder most constrains the story: regulators, government, Legal, parent-group communications, existing customers, critical urban audiences, competitors, or employees?
- How should Vivacom handle market-leader proof without inviting regulator or government attention?
- What can be said about national-critical infrastructure, satellite communications, and state services, and what must remain quarantined?
- Which past shadows resurface when a sale process is visible, and what is the approved handling line?

## D — audience & insight

What we now know:
- The first-believer audience is existing customers.
- Existing customers lived through a bumpy road including brand integrations and network migrations, with noticeable disruptions.
- Hardest audiences are existing customers and the critical urban audience, described as "the biggest influencer" for good and bad.
- Gen Z is partially being reached but needs more.
- The desired three-year association is people saying "Vivacom -- that's my telecom" or something short and warm like "my Vivacom, part of my journey."

Still to get:
- No audience research, segmentation, social listening, or sentiment evidence is supplied.
- The current beliefs of existing customers, urban critics, Gen Z, business customers, media, regulators, and employees are not established beyond the CCO's read.
- No quantified audience priority or influence/interest grid is supplied.

Questions for this set:

- Who must believe the new Vivacom story first: existing customers, critical urban audiences, Gen Z, employees, media, regulators, business customers, or parent-group stakeholders?
- What would make existing customers re-see Vivacom after brand integrations, network migrations, and service disruption memories?
- What is the emotional association Vivacom wants to create: indispensable, warm, innovative, local, useful, or personally part of people's journey?
- What does the critical urban audience currently amplify for or against Vivacom?
- What makes Gen Z only partly reached, and what proof or formats could close that gap?

## E — programme, narrative & channels

What we now know:
- Under-told stories include the repositioned advertising approach putting the person at the centre of technology.
- EON, Smart Home, and B2B Smart City solutions are under-told product and B2B stories.
- Vivacom Regional Grant and Job Lab are personally important CSR and education stories.
- The channel ambition is to tell success stories attractively, in more places and formats, so different people recognise themselves.
- The desired content stance is middle boldness: step up from moderate presence, prioritize content quality over volume, and avoid flooding channels with low-quality material.
- The desired measurement direction is a holistic instrument combining traditional presence with social-network feedback and sentiment.

Still to get:
- No final channel architecture is supplied.
- No content calendar, resourcing model, format mix, or measurement methodology is established.
- No decision is supplied on whether to mirror the client's voice or default to house style.

Questions for this set:

- Which Vivacom stories should become the first narrative pillars: EON, Smart Home, B2B Smart City, Regional Grant, Job Lab, unlimited plans, 10-gigabit network, 5G, or customer-centred advertising?
- How do we turn technical and CSR proof into a single human story rather than disconnected corporate episodes?
- Which channels should carry the step-up: earned media, LinkedIn, executive visibility, owned newsroom, social video, internal town halls, partnerships, or product PR?
- What does "more colourful, more digital, more attractive" mean in actual formats and cadence for a small comms team?
- How should Vivacom measure reputation quality across traditional presence, social feedback, and sentiment?

## F — team, culture & ways of working

What we now know:
- The experienced leadership team managing "with heart" feels true enough to keep.
- For many leaders, Vivacom "is a cause, not a career."
- Leadership should open up to the world and take active public roles in company events, industry events, and social-responsibility topics.
- The barrier is leaders stepping out, even though "they have things to say."
- The team is described as small but incredible, currently covering traditional PR channels at maximum capacity with UP's help.
- Internal communications need a clear direction communicated to nearly all employees, better-designed regular content, more energy, and formats that bring leadership closer to people.

Still to get:
- No named leadership roster, readiness map, or executive thought-leadership ownership is supplied.
- No operating model is supplied for how UP and the Corporate Communications team divide work.
- No internal communications cadence, approvals flow, or tooling constraints are detailed beyond heavy systems.

Questions for this set:

- What internal behaviour must change for Vivacom's leaders to become credible public voices?
- Which leaders are ready to step into company events, industry events, and social-responsibility topics, and which are still hesitant?
- How should internal communications become livelier despite heavy internal systems?
- What must be protected from the current culture: the experienced leadership team managing with heart, the cause-not-career commitment, and CEO-level customer engagement?
- What can the small Corporate Communications team realistically own with UP's help?

## G — constraints & guardrails (incl. AI-use / MNPI)

What we now know:
- Claims were re-audited and adapted from the start of the year with legal validation.
- Vivacom can no longer say "the only" for the 10-gig claim; it can say "the first."
- Every superlative needs a legal-proof pair.
- Vendor-migration references must not be surfaced externally.
- State-layer and national-security handling is flagged and quarantined until confirmed.
- Duct network, Recovery and Resilience Plan projects, ownership history, market-leader boasting, and ownership-transition communication all require extra care.

Still to get:
- No full legal claim register is supplied.
- No AI-use or MNPI protocol is supplied beyond the briefing pack's instruction that the leadership transition trigger is excluded from AI use.
- No approved external wording is supplied for the flagged topics.
- The "500 million" satellite/teleport reach figure is unclear and requires respondent confirmation.

Questions for this set:

- Which Vivacom claims require a legal-proof pair before use, especially around "first," "only," "widest," "best," market share, customer experience, and network quality?
- Which proof points are public-record safe, which are Legal-approved, and which are quarantined until confirmed?
- What must be excluded from AI-assisted drafting because it could involve MNPI, sale-process sensitivity, national-security sensitivity, vendor migration, or ownership-transition risk?
- What is the approved rule for using flagged state-layer, satellite/teleport, duct-network, Recovery and Resilience Plan, and ownership-history material?
- How should the team handle the competitor letter example around the single 10-gig site and the shift from "only" to "first"?

## H — logistics & decision process

What we now know:
- The CCO is the only respondent present in the supplied conversation material.
- The CCO is trying to make leaders share visionary thinking at the next town hall.
- Legal validation is required for contested claims and superlatives.
- UP is already helping a small Corporate Communications team that is at maximum capacity on traditional PR channels.

Still to get:
- Final sign-off roles from the briefing pack are not confirmed in the conversation material.
- No decision process, timetable, meeting cadence, or stakeholder interview plan is supplied.
- No owner is recorded for choosing the hypothesis to test or deciding whether to mirror client voice or use house style.

Questions for this set:

- Who signs off each layer of the work: CCO, CEO, parent-group corporate communications, Legal, Regulatory Affairs, Marketing, HR/People, or Product?
- What decision must happen first so the strategy can proceed: choose the hypothesis to test, approve the voice rule, confirm proof points, or define the stakeholder interview list?
- What is the approval path for sensitive claims and flagged topics?
- What is the timetable around the next town hall, possible sale-process milestones, and leadership visibility moments?
- What capacity can the small Corporate Communications team commit to content management and channel expansion with UP's help?

# Client Intake Brief

The single task the strategy will be built from. It is not approved until a named decision-maker approves it in writing, and nothing downstream starts before that.

## Client & context

_Who they are, business model, market(s), moment/trigger_

Vivacom is a Bulgarian telecommunications company offering mobile, fixed line, broadband internet, TV/entertainment and B2B solutions including Smart City, cloud and digital education. It is described as the incumbent and revenue market leader in a mature, saturated, price-pressured three-player market, with strong network, infrastructure and entertainment assets. The current trigger is a need to define a clearer corporate reputation story while a possible sale process and divestment due diligence are creating strategic silence inside the company.

## Organizational objective

_The one business change, and by when_

The work is intended to move Vivacom from a moderate corporate presence to a more attractive, emotional and digital reputation story built around verified proof and quality content. The desired business change is for existing customers and other stakeholders to re-see Vivacom as indispensable, innovative and personally relevant rather than as the old BTK/state-telecom incumbent. A deadline is not established, beyond a near-term need to support leadership visibility around the next town hall.

## Reputation problem / opportunity

_Current perception vs desired; the misperception to close_

At company level, Vivacom appears to have strong proof but no distinctive corporate idea: reliability, scale, infrastructure, CSR, skills work and innovation proof are present, but read as disconnected episodes. At reputation level, the problem is that Vivacom is still vulnerable to BTK legacy, ownership-history overhang, regulator sensitivity, duct-network pressure, price-indexation memory and migration disruption, while competitors are associated with clearer innovation or customer-experience claims. The opportunity is to make Vivacom feel like the telecom people personally rely on, not a heavy former utility.

## Priority audiences

_Segments + current state (know / feel / do today)_

Priority audiences named across the material are existing customers, critical urban audiences, Gen Z, media, regulators, policy and government stakeholders, talent, business customers and partners, the general public and consumer base, employees and parent-group corporate stakeholders. The clearest current-state evidence is for existing customers, who lived through brand integrations and network migrations; critical urban audiences, who are described as the biggest amplifier for good and bad; and Gen Z, which is only partly reached. Current state for the other audiences is not established with research evidence.

## Desired change

_What each audience must know, feel or do differently_

Existing customers must move from inertia and memory of a bumpy road toward saying Vivacom is doing great things and eventually feeling 'Vivacom -- that's my telecom.' Critical urban audiences need to see a more credible, attractive and emotionally relevant Vivacom instead of amplifying legacy or service frustrations. Gen Z needs to see Vivacom in more digital, colourful and relevant formats. Leaders need to move from silence to visible, credible public roles, but only within sale-process, legal and regulatory constraints.

## Stakeholders & internal alignment

_Key internal players, their wants/fears, conflicts (the Alignment Map)_

The central alignment tension is between Elitza Georgieva's wish for a more emotional, likeable, digital and visible Vivacom and leaders' reluctance to make forward-looking statements while the company is waiting for a sale and piecemeal divestment due diligence. Legal and Regulatory Affairs require every superlative and contested claim to have a proof pair. Marketing owns consumer brand and advertising budget while Corporate Communications owns reputation and PR, creating a potential ownership conflict. Competitors want access to Vivacom's legacy duct infrastructure, while Vivacom wants to protect that commercial advantage.

## Constraints & guardrails

_Commercial, regulatory, legal, do-not-say, AI/MNPI_

Claims about market share, pricing, competitive position, 'first,' 'only,' 'widest,' 'best,' customer experience and network quality require Legal/Regulatory review and proof. Vivacom can say 'first' for the 10-gigabit claim but no longer 'the only.' Vendor-migration references must not be surfaced externally. Duct network, Recovery and Resilience Plan projects, ownership history, market-leader boasting, state-layer or national-security material, satellite/teleport reach and ownership-transition communications all require extra care. The leadership transition trigger is excluded from AI use, but a full AI/MNPI protocol is not established.

## Assets & access

_Research, data, spokespeople, analytics/CRM for baselines_

The material supplies proof points including first commercial 5G network in Bulgaria, first 10-gigabit network in Bulgaria, widest high-speed footprint by cities, first unlimited consumer plans, EON, CRC indicators, Opensignal, Forbes Innovation Awards, employer recognitions, largest telecom employer status, Vivacom Regional Grant and Job Lab. It does not supply media corpus, sentiment analysis, social listening, stakeholder perception research, audience segmentation, channel analytics, CRM baselines, named stakeholder maps, legal claim register, annual reports, investor materials or confirmed analytics access.

## Success & measurement

_How success is defined; baseline, target, source, owner_

Success is defined qualitatively as lifting affinity and preference, cutting BTK/state-telecom association, making existing customers feel pride and warmth, increasing emotional and digital attractiveness, improving leadership visibility and measuring reputation quality beyond share of voice. The desired measurement direction is a holistic instrument combining traditional presence, social-network feedback and sentiment. Baselines, numeric targets, sources and measurement owners are not established.

## Scope & logistics

_Tier, budget, timeline, markets, decision-maker & approval_

The scope implies corporate positioning, proof architecture, executive thought leadership, channel programme, internal communications direction and stakeholder alignment, but the deliverable hierarchy is not finalized. The market is Bulgaria, with wider parent-group relevance. The CCO is the only respondent in the supplied debrief and the primary approval owner in the briefing pack; final sign-off is said to sit with the CEO and parent-group corporate communications, with Legal/Regulatory review for sensitive claims. Budget, tier, full timeline, meeting cadence and approval timetable are not established.

## Executive summary

1. **Vivacom's strongest raw material is proof, not personality: first 5G, first 10G, EON, fibre, CSR, employer and skills activity are present, but the supplied material says they read as disconnected episodes.**
