candidates.candidate: Vivacom's reputation problem is not that people do not know enough about its technology; it is that the proof has not yet repaired the feeling of having stayed through a bumpy relationship.
For existing customers, the most powerful Vivacom story is not innovation leadership but recognition: making them feel their choice to stay was not inertia, it was justified.
Vivacom can only become warmer by becoming more disciplined: the more emotional the story gets, the tighter the proof architecture has to be.
Vivacom has many strong proof points but no single corporate idea connecting them.
Vivacom should focus on verified proof rather than unsupported claims.
The company's first-believer audience is existing customers, because they already live with the service every day.
Critical urban audiences will not be persuaded by corporate warmth unless it comes with evidence they can repeat without feeling naive.
Gen Z does not reject Vivacom; it just does not often meet Vivacom in formats that feel made for its digital life.
The real communications enemy is not silence, but visible ambition without a claim-control system.
Vivacom should avoid a generic network-leadership fight because rivals already have clearer performance hooks.
The old incumbent identity is a liability only if Vivacom lets scale sound like dominance instead of usefulness.
Vivacom's leadership story is blocked less by lack of leaders than by the fear that visibility during sale uncertainty will create regulatory or investor risk.
The company has to stop treating CSR, skills, network and entertainment as separate news items and start treating them as evidence of one human role.
People will not give Vivacom credit for infrastructure until the company shows what that infrastructure protects in ordinary life.
The phrase 'you can't do without it' is powerful because it shifts Vivacom from a telecom supplier to a condition of modern life.
Vivacom's volume problem is that more corporate content can make the brand look busier without making it more believed.
The brand should make customers feel seen before it asks the market to see Vivacom differently.
Vivacom's biggest risk is sounding proud of the very scale some audiences associate with old monopoly power.
Legal discipline should not sit after creative work; for Vivacom it is part of the creative idea because trust is the product being rebuilt.
The market's white space is not another fastest-best-widest claim, but a telecom people feel is already there when life needs to work.
Vivacom should not try to escape BTK memory by acting like a startup; it should transform the meaning of maturity from oldness into dependability.
The audience does not need another proof point; it needs help interpreting the proof points it has already been given.
For business and public-sector stakeholders, warmth is secondary to confidence that Vivacom can deliver without service, regulatory or reputational drama.
The sale-process silence creates a paradox: Vivacom needs more visible leadership exactly when leaders have the strongest reasons to say less.
Vivacom's strongest corporate voice may be quieter than the category expects: specific, useful and evidenced rather than heroic.
A national-infrastructure story could work only if it stays personal, because political or state-layer language would activate the very sensitivities the brand needs to soften.
Existing customers are not a retention audience only; they are the credibility filter for whether the new story is believable at all.
Vivacom should measure whether people feel more pride and warmth, not just whether more people saw the brand.
The more Vivacom talks about being first, the more it must show who benefits second by second.
Vivacom's opportunity is to make Bulgarian digital progress feel less like telecom infrastructure and more like personal continuity.

cards.candidate: Vivacom's reputation problem is not that people do not know enough about its technology; it is that the proof has not yet repaired the feeling of having stayed through a bumpy relationship.
cards.insight: Vivacom is trying to win reputation credit with evidence, but its first audience is still judging it like a relationship. The proof will only work when it feels like an answer to what customers lived through, not a presentation of what the company has built.
cards.evidence: The research says existing customers are the first-believer audience, that they lived through integrations and migrations, and that they need to move from inertia and memory of a bumpy road toward feeling 'Vivacom -- that's my telecom.' It also says Vivacom has strong proof points, but they currently read as disconnected episodes.
cards.tension: Technical achievement pulls against emotional residue: Vivacom has innovation, infrastructure and service proof, but customers still carry memories of disruption, price sensitivity and old-incumbent baggage.
cards.so_what: The strategy should start with existing customers and translate proof into reassurance, recognition and pride before trying to build a broad corporate-reputation platform.
cards.audience: Existing Vivacom customers who stayed through integrations, migrations and ordinary service frustrations.
cards.opportunity: Create a reputation platform that makes service proof feel like a customer vindication story: you stayed with us, and now the value of that choice is visible in your daily life.
cards.audience_truth: They care less about whether Vivacom can list firsts and more about whether the company understands what they went through and makes staying feel like a good choice.
cards.ownable_truth: Vivacom has real, supplied proof of network, fibre, entertainment, CSR and skills activity, plus the lived fact that many customers already rely on it every day.
cards.how_contrarian: Moderately contrarian. It contradicts the instinct to lead with innovation, scale or corporate visibility, and says the first move is emotional repair with people who already know the brand.
cards.what_would_validate_it: Ask existing customers who remember migrations or service disruption to react to two story routes: one led by innovation proof, one led by recognition of their lived reliance and the value of staying. Confirmation would be: 'This feels like my experience, and it makes me feel better about being with Vivacom.' # Killer Insight Cards

30 candidates were written and screened; 3 survived; 3 are put forward as cards. Volume first, then judgment.

**Nobody has selected the insight yet.** The volume reserves that for a person: the final insight is chosen, defined and defended by a human, and this engine does not author it on autopilot.

## Card 1

**Vivacom is trying to win reputation credit with evidence, but its first audience is still judging it like a relationship. The proof will only work when it feels like an answer to what customers lived through, not a presentation of what the company has built.**

**Type.** intuitive

**The 5 T's.** True: yes · Tacit: yes · Touches the heart: yes · Tension: yes · Triggers action: yes

**The tension.** Technical achievement pulls against emotional residue: Vivacom has innovation, infrastructure and service proof, but customers still carry memories of disruption, price sensitivity and old-incumbent baggage.

**The audience it is about.** Existing Vivacom customers who stayed through integrations, migrations and ordinary service frustrations.

**The opportunity it opens.** Create a reputation platform that makes service proof feel like a customer vindication story: you stayed with us, and now the value of that choice is visible in your daily life.

**What the audience truly cares about.** They care less about whether Vivacom can list firsts and more about whether the company understands what they went through and makes staying feel like a good choice.

**The company's ownable truth.** Vivacom has real, supplied proof of network, fibre, entertainment, CSR and skills activity, plus the lived fact that many customers already rely on it every day.

**Evidence.** The research says existing customers are the first-believer audience, that they lived through integrations and migrations, and that they need to move from inertia and memory of a bumpy road toward feeling 'Vivacom -- that's my telecom.' It also says Vivacom has strong proof points, but they currently read as disconnected episodes.

**So what.** The strategy should start with existing customers and translate proof into reassurance, recognition and pride before trying to build a broad corporate-reputation platform.

## Card 2

**The emotional prize is not admiration from people at a distance; it is pride from people who already stayed. Vivacom has to turn customer inertia into customer self-respect.**

**Type.** intuitive

**The 5 T's.** True: yes · Tacit: yes · Touches the heart: yes · Tension: yes · Triggers action: yes

**The tension.** The company wants a more attractive, digital reputation story, but the customer truth starts in a less glamorous place: people stayed, sometimes through frustration, and need a reason to feel good about that.

**The audience it is about.** Existing customers with long or multi-service relationships with Vivacom.

**The opportunity it opens.** Build communications around moments where Vivacom quietly enables home, work, family, entertainment and opportunity, using concrete proof to make staying feel chosen.

**What the audience truly cares about.** They want dependable service, transparency and a reason to feel that staying with Vivacom says something sensible about them.

**The company's ownable truth.** Vivacom's role is already woven into customers' everyday connectivity, entertainment and household services; the brand can make that role visible and warmer.

**Evidence.** The approved brief names existing customers as the clearest priority audience and says they should move from inertia and memory of a bumpy road toward feeling 'Vivacom -- that's my telecom.' The CCO also identifies existing customers as the first-believer audience.

**So what.** The strategy should not treat existing customers as passive retention targets. They should become the first proof audience, with messaging that rewards their familiarity instead of trying to overwrite it.

## Card 3

**For Vivacom, emotion is not the opposite of compliance; it depends on compliance. In a trust-sensitive category, warmth without proof would make the company feel less human, not more.**

**Type.** empirical

**The 5 T's.** True: yes · Tacit: yes · Touches the heart: yes · Tension: yes · Triggers action: yes

**The tension.** Corporate Communications wants a more emotional, visible and likeable Vivacom, while Legal, Regulatory Affairs and sale-process uncertainty constrain what can safely be said.

**The audience it is about.** Critical urban audiences, media, regulators and existing customers who are alert to overclaiming, service issues or incumbent behavior.

**The opportunity it opens.** Make proof discipline part of the brand's distinctiveness: a warmer Vivacom that earns belief by being specific, verifiable and careful where the category is often loud.

**What the audience truly cares about.** They want to believe useful progress is real, but they punish telecom brands that sound evasive, inflated or disconnected from lived service experience.

**The company's ownable truth.** Vivacom has enough real proof to avoid empty emotional language, but it also has enough live sensitivities that proof cannot be optional.

**Evidence.** The research names live vulnerabilities around BTK legacy, ownership overhang, price-indexation memory, duct-network pressure, regulator sensitivity and migration disruption. The approved brief says claims about market share, pricing, competitive position, first, only, widest, best, customer experience and network quality require Legal/Regulatory review and proof.

**So what.** The strategy should build a claim-plus-proof architecture before campaign language: every emotional claim needs a supporting proof type, owner, approval path and red-line rule.

# The extraction process — seven steps

1. Immerse — absorb the research pack, the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation read
2. Generate volume — write many candidates, empirical and intuitive; do not edit yet
3. So-What ladder — push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated 'so what?'
4. Screen — test each against the five T's and discard what fails any of them
5. Find the Sweet Spot — the ownable truth, an insight not yet leveraged, what the audience truly cares about
6. Distinctiveness Gate — reject anything a competitor could also claim, or the obvious white space everyone sees
7. Distil — land one to three Killer Insights, no more

# Two kinds of insight — and why you need both

| | what it is | proven by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empirical insight | Grounded in data acquired through research methods | The data itself |
| Intuitive insight | Grounded in knowing or sensing, without a rational process | Observation and qualitative evidence — it still needs backup |

**The UP principle.** It is through science that we prove, but through intuition that we discover. The strongest Killer Insights pair an intuitive human truth with empirical proof — the discovery and the evidence together.

# The climb — from data to insight

Insight is a level on a ladder, reached by disciplined questioning — not a lucky thought.

| level | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| Data | Raw, uncontextualised facts ("sales rose 23%") |
| Information | Data organised & compared ("23% — 5 points above target, 8 below history") |
| Insight | What it means, strategically ("the growth is masking a loyalty problem") |
| Foresight | What it signals for the future ("expect margin pressure in 12 months") |

**The tool that climbs it: the So What? test.** For every finding ask "so what?" and keep asking until you reach genuine meaning. Guard against the five traps:

- correlation mistaken for causation
- confirmation bias
- volume mistaken for significance
- the missing counterfactual
- outliers mistaken for trends

# The Sweet Spot

An insight sits where all three meet:

- the company's ownable truth
- an insight not yet leveraged
- what the audience truly cares about

# Step 5B · Validate the insight

A distinctive, contrarian insight cannot lock until it is tested against the real audience. Distinctiveness and wrongness look identical until tested.

## Validating card 1

**How contrarian.** Moderately contrarian. It contradicts the instinct to lead with innovation, scale or corporate visibility, and says the first move is emotional repair with people who already know the brand.

**What would validate it.** Ask existing customers who remember migrations or service disruption to react to two story routes: one led by innovation proof, one led by recognition of their lived reliance and the value of staying. Confirmation would be: 'This feels like my experience, and it makes me feel better about being with Vivacom.' Refinement would be: 'The recognition works, but I need clearer proof on service, price or support.' Rejection would be: 'This feels like spin; my experience has not earned that emotion.'

# Strategy One-Pager

The one page everything else flows from. A gap here is a gap in the thinking.

**No approach has been chosen.** The options are below with their evaluation; the choice belongs to a person and no owner is recorded.

## Executive summary (2–3 lines)

Vivacom has enough proof to build a stronger reputation, but proof alone will not repair how people feel about the brand. The strategic task is to turn infrastructure, innovation, entertainment, CSR and skills evidence into a warmer, more credible story without outrunning legal, regulatory or lived-customer trust.

## Business & communication objectives (SMART+I)

Business objective: shift Vivacom from old-incumbent memory toward indispensable, innovative and personally relevant reputation. Communication objective: by the next town hall, align leadership around one proof-led route, one legally reviewable claim-plus-proof architecture and one existing-customer validation plan that can test warmth, pride and reduced BTK association. Measurement baselines and numeric targets are not established.

## Target audience profile & persona

Primary evidence supports existing customers as the first-believer audience, especially those who stayed through integrations, migrations and service frustrations. Critical urban audiences matter because they can amplify credibility or frustration. Gen Z is a secondary growth audience needing more digital and colourful formats. Media, regulators, policy stakeholders, employees, talent, business customers and parent-group stakeholders are named but not yet evidenced with current-state research.

## The strategic approach + one-line positioning

Three strategic routes remain open for a person to choose: Make Staying Feel Right, which closes the trust gap with existing customers; Everyday Indispensability, which repositions Vivacom around the useful role it plays in ordinary life; and Warmth That Can Be Proved, which owns the tension between emotion and compliance. The shared strategic principle is that Vivacom should not lead with unsupported admiration claims; it should make proof feel human.

## Core narrative & 3–5 key messages

Core narrative: Vivacom is not asking people to forget the bumpy road or accept another telecom leadership claim. It is showing, with specific proof, how the company people already rely on has become more useful, more modern and more personally relevant in daily life. Key messages: 1. You stayed with Vivacom, and the value of that choice should now be visible in the way your home, work, family and entertainment connect. 2. Vivacom's innovation proof matters most when it shows who benefits, not when it sits as a list of firsts. 3. A warmer Vivacom must also be a more disciplined Vivacom: every major claim needs proof, ownership and review. 4. Vivacom's scale should be framed as usefulness and dependability, not dominance or old-incumbent power. 5. Existing customers are not only a retention audience; they are the credibility filter for whether the new story is believable.

## Proof points / supporting evidence

Available proof includes first commercial 5G network in Bulgaria, first 10-gigabit network in Bulgaria, high-speed footprint by cities, EON, CRC indicators, Opensignal, Forbes Innovation Awards, employer recognitions, largest telecom employer status, Vivacom Regional Grant and Job Lab. Claims around market share, pricing, competitive position, first, only, widest, best, customer experience and network quality require Legal/Regulatory review and proof. A complete legal claim register is not established.

## Channel strategy (PESO)

PESO shape should be earned-led for corporate reputation, supported by owned proof hubs, executive and employee channels, social content and selective paid amplification only after the route is validated. Earned should lead with media-ready proof and leadership visibility; owned should house the claim-plus-proof architecture; shared should translate proof into human moments for existing customers, critical urban audiences and Gen Z; paid is not established because budget and channel baselines are missing.

## Campaign timeline & phases

The only established timing is the near-term need to support leadership visibility around the next town hall. Before that moment, the practical sequence is route choice, proof architecture, legal/regulatory red lines, leadership narrative, internal alignment and customer validation design. A full external campaign timeline is not established.

## Success metrics & KPIs

Use existing-customer warmth and pride, movement away from BTK/state-telecom association, affinity and preference, proof believability, quality of media/social response, leadership visibility quality and reputation quality beyond share of voice. Baselines, numeric targets, sources, dashboard design and measurement owners are not established.

## Budget allocation summary · risk mitigation

Budget is not established. Main risks are choosing a route before audience validation, sounding emotional without operational proof, triggering legal or regulatory issues through superlatives, overexposing leaders during sale-process uncertainty, creating ownership conflict between Corporate Communications and Marketing, and being contradicted by service, billing or migration complaints.

# The Strategy Blueprint cascade

Everything in line of sight: business objective → communication objective → strategic approach → messages, channels and tactics → KPIs.

**Business objective.** Help Vivacom shift reputation from old BTK/state-telecom incumbent toward an indispensable, innovative and personally relevant telecom, while protecting trust during sale-process, legal and regulatory sensitivities.

**Communication objective (SMART+I).** By the next town hall, equip Vivacom leadership to align on one proof-led corporate reputation route, one legally reviewable claim-plus-proof architecture and one existing-customer validation plan that can measurably test movement from inertia and bumpy-road memory toward pride, warmth and 'Vivacom -- that's my telecom.'

**How it traces.** The communication objective delivers the business outcome by turning Vivacom's existing proof into an aligned, legally defensible reputation route and testing it first with the customers whose belief must shift before broader reputation can credibly move.

# The options it was chosen from

Weak strategy is the first plausible approach written up confidently. These are the alternatives and how each scored.

## Option 1 — Make Staying Feel Right

**Shape.** Close the trust gap

**Direction.** GET existing Vivacom customers WHO stayed through integrations, migrations and ordinary service frustrations TO feel that staying was a sensible and rewarding choice BY acknowledging the bumpy road and translating Vivacom's proof into visible everyday value.

**Positioning.** Vivacom is the telecom that proves your decision to stay was worth it.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Fit | Strong fit because it directly resolves the tension between technical proof and emotional residue among the clearest first-believer audience. |
| Distinctiveness | Reasonably distinctive because competitors can claim network quality, but they cannot credibly own Vivacom customers' specific history of staying through its transformation. |
| Feasibility | Feasible because Vivacom already has proof points, daily customer reliance and a clear internal sponsor, but it needs customer validation before emotional language can be locked. |
| Durability | Durable if service proof keeps improving, but exposed in a bad news cycle if billing, support or migration issues make the recognition feel like spin. |

## Option 2 — Everyday Indispensability

**Shape.** Reposition

**Direction.** GET existing customers, critical urban audiences and the broader public WHO see Vivacom as a heavy former utility TO re-see it as the useful digital layer behind modern Bulgarian life BY connecting fibre, mobile, entertainment, skills and CSR proof to ordinary moments that need to work.

**Positioning.** Vivacom is already there when life needs to work.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Fit | Good fit because it converts disconnected proof into one human role, though it is less directly reparative than the customer-pride route. |
| Distinctiveness | Moderate because any telecom can talk about enabling life, so Vivacom would need the proof architecture and incumbent-scale transformation to make it ownable. |
| Feasibility | Feasible with existing assets across network, EON, fibre, Job Lab and community programmes, but it requires tight coordination between Corporate Communications, Marketing, Product and Legal. |
| Durability | Durable for a year if it avoids national-infrastructure boasting and stays personal, but weaker in a bad news cycle if usefulness is not backed by lived service experience. |

## Option 3 — Warmth That Can Be Proved

**Shape.** Own the tension

**Direction.** GET critical urban audiences, media, regulators and existing customers WHO are alert to overclaiming TO believe Vivacom's warmer story BY making every emotional claim specific, verifiable, carefully worded and supported by an approval-ready proof pair.

**Positioning.** Vivacom earns warmth by being precise.

| criterion | judgement |
| --- | --- |
| Fit | Strong fit for the trust-sensitive context because it makes compliance a condition of emotion rather than a barrier to it. |
| Distinctiveness | High internally and strategically, because competitors may claim proof but are less likely to make disciplined claim behavior the reputation idea itself. |
| Feasibility | Feasible only if Legal, Regulatory Affairs and Corporate Communications build a claim-plus-proof workflow before creative activation. |
| Durability | Highly durable because it can survive scrutiny and a bad news cycle better than broad emotional messaging, though it may feel less immediately inspiring unless made human. |

# Open — waiting on a person

- **Which approach do we take?** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.

# Message Architecture

One connected architecture, not three separate lists. Every message and every pillar traces back to the one story; anything that does not, does not belong.

**Not locked.** The volume gives the story truth and its tension to a person, and no owner has locked this.

## The narrative

**World.** Telecoms have become part of ordinary life in Bulgaria: work, home, family, entertainment, learning and public confidence all depend on networks that simply have to work.

**Tension.** Vivacom has real infrastructure, innovation, entertainment, employer, CSR and skills proof, but proof alone pulls against emotional residue from integrations, migrations, service frustrations and old BTK/incumbent memory. The warmer the company wants to sound, the more tightly every claim has to be evidenced.

**Resolution.** The tension resolves when Vivacom stops asking people to admire scale in the abstract and starts translating verified proof into visible everyday value, first with existing customers who can confirm whether the new story feels true.

**Our role.** Vivacom's role is to make the value of what people already rely on visible, useful and believable, with every emotional claim paired to specific proof and review.

### In the UP template

**We believe in a world where…** connection is not a background utility, but the thing that lets modern Bulgarian life keep moving.

**We know…** people do not give a telecom warmth just because it lists achievements, especially when they remember the bumpy road.

**So we make sure…** Vivacom's proof is shown through the homes, work, families, entertainment, skills and communities it helps every day.

**Which is why we…** build a warmer Vivacom story only from claims that are specific, useful, reviewable and believable to the customers who stayed.

### Compressed

**Trailer.** Vivacom is not asking people to forget the bumpy road or accept another telecom leadership claim. It is showing, with reviewable proof, how the company people already rely on has become more useful, modern and personally relevant in daily life.

**Tweet.** Vivacom's warmer story cannot come from softer words alone. It has to show existing customers that staying makes sense, turning network, fibre, EON, CSR and skills proof into everyday value they can actually recognize.

## Key messages

Each message laddered: the umbrella claim, the pillar that holds it up, and the specific proof.

| message | audience | type | pillar | 1° umbrella | 2° supporting | 3° killer fact | do not say |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Communications pillars

The few enduring territories, each tracing to the narrative, balanced across Hero ~20%, Hub ~60%, Hygiene ~20%.

### Customer proof that makes staying feel right

**Traces to.** Carries the tension between technical proof and emotional residue, and the resolution that existing customers must feel the value of staying.

**Hero.** A few major customer-recognition stories that acknowledge the bumpy road and show how Vivacom now helps homes, families, work and entertainment run better.

**Hub.** Ongoing existing-customer proof stories: everyday connection moments, service improvements, EON usage, fibre benefits, family and work scenarios, and customer validation learnings.

**Hygiene.** Clear proof explainers, claim sources, service information, FAQ-style reassurance and legally reviewed customer-benefit wording.

**Story types.** Evergreen, Seasonal, Real-time Reactive

### Useful scale in everyday Bulgarian life

**Traces to.** Carries the world and resolution: telecom scale matters when it is seen as everyday usefulness rather than dominance.

**Hero.** Big earned-led reputation moments showing Vivacom's role in modern Bulgarian life without national-infrastructure boasting.

**Hub.** City, household, work, entertainment, education and community stories that translate footprint, EON, CSR and skills programmes into ordinary usefulness.

**Hygiene.** Owned proof hubs, city-by-city availability context, sourced claim pages and simple explainers for what Vivacom enables.

**Story types.** Evergreen, Seasonal

### Innovation translated into human benefit

**Traces to.** Carries the resolution that innovation proof must show who benefits, not just what Vivacom built.

**Hero.** Selective innovation stories around 5G, 10-gigabit, EON or awards, framed through concrete audience benefit and approved proof.

**Hub.** Regular product, network, entertainment, skills and business-customer stories that answer what changed for people because of the innovation.

**Hygiene.** Reviewed innovation proof pairs, definitions, technical explainers and source notes for claims that may trigger scrutiny.

**Story types.** Evergreen, Real-time Reactive

### Warmth with proof discipline

**Traces to.** Carries the role: Vivacom can become warmer only by being more specific, verifiable and careful.

**Hero.** Leadership and corporate reputation moments that demonstrate a warmer tone through precise, proof-paired claims.

**Hub.** Claim-plus-proof content, executive visibility with review, media-ready evidence, employee alignment and legal/regulatory workflow stories.

**Hygiene.** Claim register, approval rules, red-line guidance, proof ownership and review notes for sensitive wording.

**Story types.** Evergreen, Real-time Reactive

## Do-not-say guardrails

| do not say | why |
| --- | --- |
| Do not ask people to forget the bumpy road or accept another telecom leadership claim. | The material says Vivacom must not outrun lived customer trust, migration memories or the old-incumbent association. |
| Do not lead with unsupported admiration claims. | The strategic principle says Vivacom should not lead with unsupported admiration claims; it should make proof feel human. |
| Do not use unreviewed claims about market share, pricing, competitive position, first, only, widest, best, customer experience or network quality. | The proof section says these claim areas require Legal/Regulatory review and proof, and a complete legal claim register is not established. |
| Do not frame scale as dominance, old-incumbent power, national-infrastructure boasting or political/state-layer language. | The material says Vivacom's scale should be framed as usefulness and dependability, not dominance or old-incumbent power, and warns against activating state-layer sensitivities. |
| Do not overexpose leaders during sale-process uncertainty. | The risk section names leader overexposure during sale-process uncertainty as a reputational risk. |
| Do not make emotional claims without specific proof, ownership and review. | The material says warmth must be proof-led and every major claim needs proof, ownership and review. |

## The Content Strategy Cascade

Narrative → Themes → Stories → Sequencing.

## The content balance

Described at all three levels without the proportions, a pillar reads as three equal commitments. It is not — the middle carries the programme.

| level | share and what it is |
| --- | --- |
| Hero | ~20% — the few big moments |
| Hub | ~60% — ongoing content that builds audience and demonstrates the pillars |
| Hygiene | ~20% — the always-on answers people actually search for |

# UP Strategy Input Readiness Packet

Use this packet before strategy work begins to decide whether the team can proceed or must re-brief, pause, or escalate.

## Review Metadata

- Source-backed records: 14
- Manager findings: 0
- Exact source quotes: 14 / 14
- Category coverage: governance_input=4, missing_input_response=4, quality_gate=3, required_input=3

## Required Inputs

Inputs that must exist before the workflow can proceed with confidence.

- `up-input-001` required_input: Corporate decision-maker authority must be confirmed in writing at kickoff.
  Reason: The source requires written confirmation of sign-off authority at kickoff and does not state a separate pre-kickoff readiness acceptance point.
  Evidence: Corporate decision-maker authority confirmed in writing | AM, escalated to CEO | Corporate strategies must have CEO-level or Communications Director-level sign-off authority confirmed at kickoff.
- `up-input-002` required_input: Annual report, investor materials, or private-company equivalent governance materials are required.
  Reason: The source explicitly labels these materials as required and non-negotiable for listed clients.
  Evidence: Most recent annual report and investor materials | Client | Required. If the client is publicly listed, this is non-negotiable. If private, equivalent governance/board materials are required.
- `up-input-003` required_input: An initial stakeholder universe list must be provided and validated by the client, then expanded via dedicated mapping in Phase 2.
  Reason: The source identifies the stakeholder universe as an input, says the initial list comes from the client and is validated by the client, and says the workflow expands it in Phase 2.
  Evidence: Stakeholder universe — known and unknown | AM, validated by client | Initial stakeholder list from client; this workflow expands it via dedicated mapping in Phase 2.

## Quality Gates

Thresholds that decide whether inputs are usable.

- `up-input-004` quality_gate: Corporate strategy input quality is treated as directly tied to strategic accuracy.
  Reason: The source states the quality gate principle and links poor inputs to inaccurate strategy.
  Evidence: Quality gate principle, intensified. For corporate work, input quality directly correlates with strategic accuracy.
- `up-input-005` quality_gate: Strategy Lead may veto proceeding when input quality is insufficient.
  Reason: The source explicitly grants hard veto authority over input quality.
  Evidence: Strategy Lead has hard veto authority on input quality.
- `up-input-013` quality_gate: Strategy work must surface gaps and unresolved positioning before drafting.
  Reason: The brief defines input discipline as part of what good looks like.
  Evidence: Input discipline: surfaces gaps before writing and flags that positioning is undecided.

## Missing Input Response

Actions required when inputs are missing, weak, or strategically unsafe.

- `up-input-006` missing_input_response: If the brief is wrong, incomplete, or omits material risk, the workflow pauses and re-engages the client.
  Reason: The source defines the required response when missing or undisclosed input is discovered.
  Evidence: If research reveals the original brief was wrong or incomplete on corporate matters — particularly if a material risk or regulatory issue surfaces that the client did not disclose at kickoff — the Strategy Lead pauses and re-engages the client.

payload.markdown:
# Strategy Brief

## Evidence Readiness And Gaps
- UP analysis: The evidence is strong enough for a first message architecture, not strong enough for a locked public platform. The platform is not locked.
- Known input readiness: Corporate decision-maker authority confirmed in writing; ESG / sustainability disclosures and CSRD readiness status; Regulatory environment briefing; AI-use limits are present for this sanitized demo.
- Known operating reality: The client is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group. Mass-market consumer is the revenue core. B2B, enterprise, and public-sector solutions are strategic growth areas.
- Missing inputs: no current reputation baseline, no complete CEO or parent-group view, no Legal/Regulatory Affairs answer set, no confirmed attribution model, and several R-VERIFY or FLAG claims still need evidence owner confirmation.
- Proof ladder, strongest first: named client reference > anonymized-but-verifiable case > technical artifact > internal demo. Any reviewable example must sit on this ladder; an internal demo cannot be treated as third-party validation.
- UP analysis: Claims near regulation, market leadership, critical infrastructure, pricing, data handling, ESG, or certification must describe practice and discipline only. They must not imply certification, market authority, or regulatory status unless Legal/Regulatory Affairs and the evidence owner approve the exact wording.

## What Your Answers Changed
- Resolved by the interview: the human line moved forward. The client-supplied language is “You can’t do without it.” and “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
- Resolved by the interview: the first audience moved toward existing customers, because the respondent named “Existing customers” and described the desired reaction as “these people are doing great things”.
- Resolved by the interview: the do-not-say list became sharper. “the BTK” is categorically out, and broad market-leader boasting is a regulatory risk.
- Resolved by the interview: measurement cannot stop at share of voice; the respondent said share of voice is no longer enough and wants a more holistic instrument.
- Still open: the public core line, proof threshold, first audience lock, founder and leadership visibility roles, signature-language variant, and claim disposition for high-risk superlatives.
- UP analysis: The recommended spine moved from a discovery-stage scale-and-leadership territory toward a human-usefulness interim lead, with a critical-capability territory developed only after proof clears the ladder.

## Strategic Problem To Solve
- Known facts: Market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator. Operationally strong, with leading network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets. The category is trusted but not loved, and the company is respected but lacks a distinctive corporate idea.
- Missing inputs: reputation baseline by stakeholder, customer trust and preference baseline, employee alignment baseline, CEO and parent-group confirmation, Legal/Regulatory Affairs proof thresholds, and the final public role of leadership.
- UP-inferred, not client-named: this is Enterprise-primary corporate reputation work because approval, regulator exposure, parent-group involvement, and proof governance matter more than headcount.
- UP-inferred, not client-named: the primary reputation battleground for the first 6-12 months is hybrid but B2C-led, because mass-market consumer perception appears to be where reputation value first converts; B2B and public-sector credibility should support, not replace, that first battleground.
- UP analysis: This fork logic is United Partners' operating framework, consistent with AMEC's stakeholder-first orientation, not based on an external standard.

## Open Positioning Decisions
- Core line choice A - indispensability: use “You can’t do without it.” as the internal pressure-test line, not automatic public copy. Consequence: strongest distinctiveness, highest proof and regulator burden.
- Core line choice B - human usefulness: lead with “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”. Consequence: safest interim public platform because it connects services to people without claiming monopoly or certification.
- Core line choice C - warm belonging: develop “Vivacom — that’s my telecom” or “my Vivacom, part of my journey” as future signature language. Consequence: strongest affinity route, but it needs customer-language validation before it becomes the corporate line.
- First audience choice A - existing customers: prioritize people who lived through the bumpy road and need a reason to re-see the brand. Consequence: reputation repair starts where lived experience is hardest to change.
- First audience choice B - critical urban audience: prioritize the audience the respondent called “the biggest influencer”. Consequence: faster cultural signal, higher scrutiny, and greater need for digital-platform discipline.
- First audience choice C - employee and leadership alignment: start inside with a clearer direction and leadership contact. Consequence: slower external lift, stronger internal permission to speak with one voice.
- Proof threshold choice A - legal-proof pair for every superlative: require evidence owner plus Legal/Regulatory Affairs approval before any first, best, biggest, widest, most, market-leader, or only-adjacent wording goes external. Consequence: lowest regulatory risk and slower copy approval.
- Proof threshold choice B - ladder proof before narrative proof points: allow narrative pillars once proof sits on the ladder, while holding superlatives for later. Consequence: faster platform build, but limited public proof language.
- Leadership role choice A - visible advocates: leadership takes active public roles in company events, industry events, and social-responsibility topics. Consequence: strongest trust transfer, but it remains unconfirmed until the named leaders accept the role.
- Leadership role choice B - internal-first leadership: leadership starts with town hall, employee formats, and informal contact before public executive profiling. Consequence: stronger alignment before external visibility, slower media presence.
- Signature language choice A - preserve “You can’t do without it.”. Consequence: sharpest owner-language signal, but public use needs proof and regulatory review.
- Signature language choice B - preserve “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”. Consequence: warmest human-benefit signal and easiest bridge to campaigns.
- Signature language choice C - preserve “Vivacom — that’s my telecom”. Consequence: strongest belonging signal, but needs audience validation before house phrasing.

## Positioning Options
1. Human usefulness platform: the company that helps people “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”. UP analysis: this is the best interim public lead because it is human, useful, and not dependent on the most sensitive leadership or infrastructure claims.
2. Critical capability stewardship: the trusted operator of essential communications capability. UP analysis: this territory is strategically powerful but must be developed with regulator-aware proof and careful avoidance of former-monopoly framing.
3. Smart-city and public-service partner for regulated digital progress: a narrower vertical territory for municipalities, enterprises, and public-sector-adjacent services. UP analysis: this is the orthogonal who-for option; proof is thinner, but narrowing the territory could let a smaller evidence base dominate a niche if B2B Smart City and public-service proof clears the ladder.

## Recommended Direction And Rationale
- Interim public lead: human usefulness. Lead with the people-centred idea already present in the respondent's words: “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
- Direction to develop: critical capability stewardship, promoted only when the proof base is technical-artifact tier or stronger and Legal/Regulatory Affairs approves the exact claim language.
- Do not lead publicly with the unprovable. “leads the market with every innovation of recent years” is internal owner language only until it clears technical-artifact proof and claim-discipline review.
- UP analysis: the recommendation is proof-sequenced, not a fallback. Current proof can support a human-usefulness story; future proof may support a more ambitious national digital-capability story.

## Message Architecture First Build
- Core idea to test: “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
- Pillar 1 - Human usefulness: communications should show the person at the centre of the technology, using examples such as “fast internet so you can run the marathon and stay connected to your family”.
- Pillar 2 - Proof-led innovation: use verified proof only, starting with claims such as First commercial 5G network in Bulgaria, First to offer 10-gigabit speeds on the Bulgarian market, and First unlimited consumer plans in Bulgaria only after evidence owner and Legal/Regulatory Affairs approval.
- Pillar 3 - Critical capability stewardship: speak about continuity, resilience, and public importance without implying certification, state status, or former-monopoly entitlement.
- Pillar 4 - Leadership with heart: develop the respondent's language about leadership managing “with heart” and Vivacom as “is a cause, not a career”, but confirm CEO and parent-group alignment before public executive profiling.
- Audience proof points: existing customers need proof that service disruption is not the story; employees need a clear shared direction; regulators need disciplined wording; B2B and public-sector audiences need verified examples, not broad claims.

## Pillar Architecture Rationale
- Human usefulness proof base: “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”, “fast internet so you can run the marathon and stay connected to your family”, and “in a cool, likeable way”. UP analysis: this pillar has the cleanest path because it does not require a market-leader claim.
- Proof-led innovation proof base: First commercial 5G network in Bulgaria; First to offer 10-gigabit speeds on the Bulgarian market; First unlimited consumer plans in Bulgaria. UP analysis: every item stays R-VERIFY until the legal-proof pair is attached.
- Critical capability stewardship proof base: critical state services run over Vivacom and sole operator for the satellite communications / teleport stations hosting major global players and secured state communications. UP analysis: this proof collides with the do-not-say risk around state-utility framing, so the reframe is stewardship of critical capability, not incumbent scale or former-monopoly reach.
- Leadership with heart proof base: “with heart”, “is a cause, not a career”, and “They have things to say”. UP analysis: this becomes a public leadership pillar only if the named leaders accept public roles.

## Risks And Guardrails
- Quarantined public-copy language: “leads the market with every innovation of recent years” is too broad for public use until supported at technical-artifact tier or above and reviewed for legal-regulatory risk.
- Quarantined public-copy language: “the best TV on the planet” is emotional respondent language, not usable proof or signature language.
- Do not say: “the BTK”. UP analysis: this is a hard identity guardrail, not a stylistic preference.
- Do not imply certification or regulatory status from practice language. “We handle data carefully” is not “we are compliant”.
- Any market-leader, first, only, widest, largest, best, or most claim needs a legal-proof pair owned by the evidence owner and approved by Legal/Regulatory Affairs.
- Sensitive material stays internal unless separately cleared: vendor migration, duct network, Recovery and Resilience Plan projects, ownership-history overhang, price-indexation scandal, and the “500 million” reach figure.

# Strategy Brief

## Evidence Readiness And Gaps
- UP analysis: The evidence is strong enough for a first message architecture, not strong enough for a locked public platform. <!-- CLAIM:c-platform-not-locked -->The platform is not locked<!-- /CLAIM:c-platform-not-locked -->.
- Known input readiness: <!-- CLAIM:c-corporate-decision-maker -->Corporate decision-maker authority confirmed in writing<!-- /CLAIM:c-corporate-decision-maker -->; <!-- CLAIM:c-esg-csrd -->ESG / sustainability disclosures and CSRD readiness status<!-- /CLAIM:c-esg-csrd -->; <!-- CLAIM:c-regulatory-briefing -->Regulatory environment briefing<!-- /CLAIM:c-regulatory-briefing -->; AI-use limits are present for this sanitized demo.
- Known operating reality: <!-- CLAIM:c-subsidiary -->The client is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group<!-- /CLAIM:c-subsidiary -->. <!-- CLAIM:c-mass-market-core -->Mass-market consumer is the revenue core<!-- /CLAIM:c-mass-market-core -->. <!-- CLAIM:c-b2b-growth -->B2B, enterprise, and public-sector solutions are strategic growth areas<!-- /CLAIM:c-b2b-growth -->.
- Missing inputs: no current reputation baseline, no complete CEO or parent-group view, no Legal/Regulatory Affairs answer set, no confirmed attribution model, and several R-VERIFY or FLAG claims still need evidence owner confirmation.
- Proof ladder, strongest first: named client reference > anonymized-but-verifiable case > technical artifact > internal demo. Any reviewable example must sit on this ladder; an internal demo cannot be treated as third-party validation.
- UP analysis: Claims near regulation, market leadership, critical infrastructure, pricing, data handling, ESG, or certification must describe practice and discipline only. They must not imply certification, market authority, or regulatory status unless Legal/Regulatory Affairs and the evidence owner approve the exact wording.

## What Your Answers Changed
- Resolved by the interview: the human line moved forward. The client-supplied language is “You can’t do without it.” and “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
- Resolved by the interview: the first audience moved toward existing customers, because the respondent named “Existing customers” and described the desired reaction as “these people are doing great things”.
- Resolved by the interview: the do-not-say list became sharper. “the BTK” is categorically out, and broad market-leader boasting is a regulatory risk.
- Resolved by the interview: measurement cannot stop at share of voice; the respondent said share of voice is no longer enough and wants a more holistic instrument.
- Still open: the public core line, proof threshold, first audience lock, founder and leadership visibility roles, signature-language variant, and claim disposition for high-risk superlatives.
- UP analysis: The recommended spine moved from a discovery-stage scale-and-leadership territory toward a human-usefulness interim lead, with a critical-capability territory developed only after proof clears the ladder.

## Strategic Problem To Solve
- Known facts: <!-- CLAIM:c-market-leader-revenue -->Market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator<!-- /CLAIM:c-market-leader-revenue -->. <!-- CLAIM:c-operationally-strong -->Operationally strong, with leading network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets<!-- /CLAIM:c-operationally-strong -->. The category is trusted but not loved, and the company is respected but lacks a distinctive corporate idea.
- Missing inputs: reputation baseline by stakeholder, customer trust and preference baseline, employee alignment baseline, CEO and parent-group confirmation, Legal/Regulatory Affairs proof thresholds, and the final public role of leadership.
- UP-inferred, not client-named: this is Enterprise-primary corporate reputation work because approval, regulator exposure, parent-group involvement, and proof governance matter more than headcount.
- UP-inferred, not client-named: the primary reputation battleground for the first 6-12 months is hybrid but B2C-led, because mass-market consumer perception appears to be where reputation value first converts; B2B and public-sector credibility should support, not replace, that first battleground.
- UP analysis: This fork logic is United Partners' operating framework, consistent with AMEC's stakeholder-first orientation, not based on an external standard.

## Open Positioning Decisions
- Core line choice A - indispensability: use “You can’t do without it.” as the internal pressure-test line, not automatic public copy. Consequence: strongest distinctiveness, highest proof and regulator burden.
- Core line choice B - human usefulness: lead with “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”. Consequence: safest interim public platform because it connects services to people without claiming monopoly or certification.
- Core line choice C - warm belonging: develop “Vivacom — that’s my telecom” or “my Vivacom, part of my journey” as future signature language. Consequence: strongest affinity route, but it needs customer-language validation before it becomes the corporate line.
- First audience choice A - existing customers: prioritize people who lived through the bumpy road and need a reason to re-see the brand. Consequence: reputation repair starts where lived experience is hardest to change.
- First audience choice B - critical urban audience: prioritize the audience the respondent called “the biggest influencer”. Consequence: faster cultural signal, higher scrutiny, and greater need for digital-platform discipline.
- First audience choice C - employee and leadership alignment: start inside with a clearer direction and leadership contact. Consequence: slower external lift, stronger internal permission to speak with one voice.
- Proof threshold choice A - legal-proof pair for every superlative: require evidence owner plus Legal/Regulatory Affairs approval before any first, best, biggest, widest, most, market-leader, or only-adjacent wording goes external. Consequence: lowest regulatory risk and slower copy approval.
- Proof threshold choice B - ladder proof before narrative proof points: allow narrative pillars once proof sits on the ladder, while holding superlatives for later. Consequence: faster platform build, but limited public proof language.
- Leadership role choice A - visible advocates: leadership takes active public roles in company events, industry events, and social-responsibility topics. Consequence: strongest trust transfer, but it remains unconfirmed until the named leaders accept the role.
- Leadership role choice B - internal-first leadership: leadership starts with town hall, employee formats, and informal contact before public executive profiling. Consequence: stronger alignment before external visibility, slower media presence.
- Signature language choice A - preserve “You can’t do without it.”. Consequence: sharpest owner-language signal, but public use needs proof and regulatory review.
- Signature language choice B - preserve “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”. Consequence: warmest human-benefit signal and easiest bridge to campaigns.
- Signature language choice C - preserve “Vivacom — that’s my telecom”. Consequence: strongest belonging signal, but needs audience validation before house phrasing.

## Positioning Options
1. Human usefulness platform: the company that helps people “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”. UP analysis: this is the best interim public lead because it is human, useful, and not dependent on the most sensitive leadership or infrastructure claims.
2. Critical capability stewardship: the trusted operator of essential communications capability. UP analysis: this territory is strategically powerful but must be developed with regulator-aware proof and careful avoidance of former-monopoly framing.
3. Smart-city and public-service partner for regulated digital progress: a narrower vertical territory for municipalities, enterprises, and public-sector-adjacent services. UP analysis: this is the orthogonal who-for option; proof is thinner, but narrowing the territory could let a smaller evidence base dominate a niche if B2B Smart City and public-service proof clears the ladder.

## Recommended Direction And Rationale
- Interim public lead: human usefulness. Lead with the people-centred idea already present in the respondent's words: “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
- Direction to develop: critical capability stewardship, promoted only when the proof base is technical-artifact tier or stronger and Legal/Regulatory Affairs approves the exact claim language.
- Do not lead publicly with the unprovable. “<!-- CLAIM:c-leads-every-innovation -->leads the market with every innovation of recent years<!-- /CLAIM:c-leads-every-innovation -->” is internal owner language only until it clears technical-artifact proof and claim-discipline review.
- UP analysis: the recommendation is proof-sequenced, not a fallback. Current proof can support a human-usefulness story; future proof may support a more ambitious national digital-capability story.

## Message Architecture First Build
- Core idea to test: “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
- Pillar 1 - Human usefulness: communications should show the person at the centre of the technology, using examples such as “fast internet so you can run the marathon and stay connected to your family”.
- Pillar 2 - Proof-led innovation: use verified proof only, starting with claims such as <!-- CLAIM:c-first-5g -->First commercial 5G network in Bulgaria<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-5g -->, <!-- CLAIM:c-first-10g-offer -->First to offer 10-gigabit speeds on the Bulgarian market<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-10g-offer -->, and <!-- CLAIM:c-first-unlimited -->First unlimited consumer plans in Bulgaria<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-unlimited --> only after evidence owner and Legal/Regulatory Affairs approval.
- Pillar 3 - Critical capability stewardship: speak about continuity, resilience, and public importance without implying certification, state status, or former-monopoly entitlement.
- Pillar 4 - Leadership with heart: develop the respondent's language about leadership managing “with heart” and Vivacom as “is a cause, not a career”, but confirm CEO and parent-group alignment before public executive profiling.
- Audience proof points: existing customers need proof that service disruption is not the story; employees need a clear shared direction; regulators need disciplined wording; B2B and public-sector audiences need verified examples, not broad claims.

## Pillar Architecture Rationale
- Human usefulness proof base: “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”, “fast internet so you can run the marathon and stay connected to your family”, and “in a cool, likeable way”. UP analysis: this pillar has the cleanest path because it does not require a market-leader claim.
- Proof-led innovation proof base: <!-- CLAIM:c-first-5g -->First commercial 5G network in Bulgaria<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-5g -->; <!-- CLAIM:c-first-10g-offer -->First to offer 10-gigabit speeds on the Bulgarian market<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-10g-offer -->; <!-- CLAIM:c-first-unlimited -->First unlimited consumer plans in Bulgaria<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-unlimited -->. UP analysis: every item stays R-VERIFY until the legal-proof pair is attached.
- Critical capability stewardship proof base: <!-- CLAIM:qaf-89eb35a88a1d128a -->critical state services run over Vivacom<!-- /CLAIM:qaf-89eb35a88a1d128a --> and <!-- CLAIM:c-sole-satellite -->sole operator for the satellite communications / teleport stations hosting major global players and secured state communications<!-- /CLAIM:c-sole-satellite -->. UP analysis: this proof collides with the do-not-say risk around state-utility framing, so the reframe is stewardship of critical capability, not incumbent scale or former-monopoly reach.
- Leadership with heart proof base: “with heart”, “is a cause, not a career”, and “They have things to say”. UP analysis: this becomes a public leadership pillar only if the named leaders accept public roles.

## By Dimension
How to read this section: quoted bullets are verbatim respondent language and UP analysis lines are United Partners commentary, never respondent language.

Purpose - strong: the interview supplies both an indispensable-role phrase and a human-benefit purpose.
- “You can’t do without it.”
- “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”
UP analysis: Purpose is usable for architecture, but the public core line remains unlocked.

Differentiation - moderate: differentiation is supported by proof claims but the respondent also admitted the only-us line is not fully settled.
- “I’m not sure I can claim to have such an answer.”
- “<!-- CLAIM:c-changed-sector -->changed the telecom sector and move it forward<!-- /CLAIM:c-changed-sector -->”
UP analysis: Differentiation must be proof-led and legally reviewed.

Proof - thin by tier: many proof points are named, but many are marked R-VERIFY or FLAG.
- “<!-- CLAIM:c-first-5g -->First commercial 5G network in Bulgaria<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-5g -->”
- “<!-- CLAIM:c-first-10g-offer -->First to offer 10-gigabit speeds on the Bulgarian market<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-10g-offer -->”
- “<!-- CLAIM:c-first-unlimited -->First unlimited consumer plans in Bulgaria<!-- /CLAIM:c-first-unlimited -->”
UP analysis: proof exists as leads, not yet as cleared public copy.

Reputation - strong: the respondent gave desired associations, customer repair, and risk overhangs.
- “these people are doing great things”
- “Vivacom — that’s my telecom”
UP analysis: reputation should be rebuilt from customer lived experience, not only media presence.

Ambition - moderate: the desired energy is clear, but shared leadership vision is not.
- “We lack a clearly stated, inspiring, shared strategic vision.”
- “more colourful, more digital, more attractive.”
UP analysis: ambition needs CEO and parent-group confirmation before lock.

Risk - strong: the interview clearly identifies claim, regulator, ownership, infrastructure, vendor-migration, and legacy-identity risks.
- “the BTK”
- “the only”
- “life and death”
UP analysis: risk discipline must shape the language before creative development.

Stakeholders - moderate: existing customers and critical urban audiences are named; regulators and parent group are implied by risk and approval chain.
- “Existing customers.”
- “the biggest influencer”
UP analysis: stakeholder priority is directionally clear but still needs owner lock.

Alignment - thin: the respondent reports lack of shared vision, but no other leaders have answered.
- “We lack a clearly stated, inspiring, shared strategic vision.”
UP analysis: alignment is unconfirmed until CEO, Legal/Regulatory Affairs, Marketing, HR/People, Product, and parent-group communications respond.

Narrative - moderate: several story routes are present, especially human-centred technology and content management.
- “fast internet so you can run the marathon and stay connected to your family”
- “not ‘we installed CCTV in Pleven’ — the why behind it”
UP analysis: narrative should be built from specific human moments, not activity listings.

Signature language - strong but unresolved variance: the interview supplies several repeatable phrases, and UP must not merge them silently.
- “You can’t do without it.”
- “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”
- “Vivacom — that’s my telecom”
- “my Vivacom, part of my journey.”
UP analysis: the house phrase is an owner decision, not a writer decision.

owner_questions.question: Which public core line should the platform lock first: indispensability, human usefulness, or warm belonging?

guide_grounding.label_quote: Core line choice A - indispensability
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: strongest distinctiveness, highest proof and regulator burden.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Core line choice B - human usefulness
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: safest interim public platform because it connects services to people without claiming monopoly or certification.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Core line choice C - warm belonging
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: strongest affinity route, but it needs customer-language validation before it becomes the corporate line.

owner_questions.question: Which first audience should the first 6-12 months prioritize: existing customers, critical urban audience, or employee and leadership alignment?

guide_grounding.label_quote: First audience choice A - existing customers
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: reputation repair starts where lived experience is hardest to change.

guide_grounding.label_quote: First audience choice B - critical urban audience
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: faster cultural signal, higher scrutiny, and greater need for digital-platform discipline.

guide_grounding.label_quote: First audience choice C - employee and leadership alignment
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: slower external lift, stronger internal permission to speak with one voice.

owner_questions.question: What proof threshold must clear before any first, best, biggest, widest, most, market-leader, or only-adjacent claim goes external?

guide_grounding.label_quote: Proof threshold choice A - legal-proof pair for every superlative
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: lowest regulatory risk and slower copy approval.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Proof threshold choice B - ladder proof before narrative proof points
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: faster platform build, but limited public proof language.

owner_questions.question: Which leadership visibility role should each leader accept before executive profiling moves from internal alignment to public activation?

guide_grounding.label_quote: Leadership role choice A - visible advocates
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: strongest trust transfer, but it remains unconfirmed until the named leaders accept the role.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Leadership role choice B - internal-first leadership
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: stronger alignment before external visibility, slower media presence.

owner_questions.question: Should “leads the market with every innovation of recent years” be retired, reworked after legal proof, or quarantined from public copy?

guide_grounding.label_quote: Quarantined public-copy language
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: “<!-- CLAIM:c-leads-every-innovation -->leads the market with every innovation of recent years<!-- /CLAIM:c-leads-every-innovation -->” is too broad for public use until supported at technical-artifact tier or above and reviewed for legal-regulatory risk.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Do not lead publicly with the unprovable
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: “<!-- CLAIM:c-leads-every-innovation -->leads the market with every innovation of recent years<!-- /CLAIM:c-leads-every-innovation -->” is internal owner language only until it clears technical-artifact proof and claim-discipline review.

owner_questions.question: Which signature-language variant becomes house phrasing: “You can’t do without it.”, “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”, or “Vivacom — that’s my telecom”?

guide_grounding.label_quote: Signature language choice A - preserve “You can’t do without it.”
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: sharpest owner-language signal, but public use needs proof and regulatory review.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Signature language choice B - preserve “do what matters most to them, in the best possible way”.
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: warmest human-benefit signal and easiest bridge to campaigns.

guide_grounding.label_quote: Signature language choice C - preserve “Vivacom — that’s my telecom”.
guide_grounding.consequence_quote: Consequence: strongest belonging signal, but needs audience validation before house phrasing.
